query:
Survey the PATENT literature and COMMERCIAL products for aluminium alloys designed for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) and related powder routes, so that we can choose starting compositions for an alloy discovery campaign and know what is already claimed. We want published compositions, not marketing.

For each entry give: assignee / vendor, product name if any, patent or application numbers (US, EP, WO, CN, JP, DE), priority year, the claimed composition RANGES and the worked EXAMPLE compositions (wt%), the cracking-control and strengthening mechanism claimed, recommended heat treatment, the properties reported in the patent or datasheet (yield, UTS, elongation, hardness, conductivity, test orientation), and whether the patent is granted, pending, expired or abandoned where known.

Cover at least:
1. Airbus / APWorks Scalmalloy (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr-Mn), and the earlier Al-Mg-Sc family patents; lower-Sc or Sc-free variants claimed by others.
2. HRL Laboratories 7A77 and Zr / grain-refiner functionalized 7xxx, 6xxx, 2xxx powders.
3. Aeromet / Aluminium Materials Technologies A20X (A205; Al-Cu-Ag-Mg-Ti-B).
4. NanoAl / Unity Aluminum / Braidy Addalloy (Al-Mg-Zr and others) and Northwestern University Al-Zr-(Er, Sc, Yb, Si) patents.
5. Constellium Aheadd CP1 (Al-Fe-Zr) and HT1 (Al-Ni-Mn-Cu-Zr-Fe class), and the C-TEC patent families (Al-Zr, Al-Fe-Zr, Al-Ni-Zr, Al-Mn-Zr, Al-Cr-Zr).
6. Fehrmann AlMgty (Al-Mg-Si / high-Mg), Rheinfelden (Magsimal, Castasil, Castaduct for AM), AMAG, Hydro, Trimet.
7. Elementum 3D A1000-RAM, A2024-RAM2, A6061-RAM2, A7050-RAM2 (reactive additive manufacturing, in-situ ceramic inoculants).
8. Rusal / IL&M (RS-230, RS-300, RS-320, RS-333, RS-390, RS-553 and similar: Al-Si-Mg-Cu, Al-Mg-Sc, Al-Ni-Mn-Fe-Zr, Al-Cu-Ce), with compositions.
9. Monash University / Amaero high-strength Al-Mn-Sc ("HOT Al"), and Al-Mg-Si-Sc-Zr.
10. Chalmers / Hoganas Al-Mn-Cr-Zr; Hoganas forAM Al grades; Kymera / ECKA / AP&C / Equispheres / Valimet / Carpenter / Sandvik / Toyal / Eckart (e.g. Eckart TiB2- or Zr-modified, Toyal Hyper-Al) aluminium AM powders with published chemistries.
11. Oak Ridge / Eck Industries / Ames Al-Ce alloys (Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Ce-Ni-Mn, Al-Cu-Mn-Zr / ACMZ, DuAlumin-3D), Lawrence Livermore Al-Ce.
12. Alcoa / Arconic / Howmet AM aluminium (Al-Fe-V-Si, Al-Ni, Al-Mn, "A1000" class), QuesTek Al for AM (Sc-free, high-temperature), Citrine / HRL / NASA collaborations, NASA 7xxx / GRCop is out of scope.
13. Japanese and Korean filings: Toyo Aluminium, Daido, Kobe Steel, UACJ, Nippon Light Metal, Sumitomo, Hitachi Metals, Toyota (Al-Fe, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Ni-Co, Al-Mn-Cr, Al-Si-Mg-Mn high-Mg).
14. Chinese filings and products: CRRC / Central South University Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, Al-Mg-Er-Zr (Beijing University of Technology Er-microalloying patents), Al-Mn-Mg-Er-Zr, TiB2/AlSi10Mg (Shanghai Jiao Tong), Al-Zn-Mg-Sc-Zr, Sc-free high-strength Al for AM.
15. EOS (Al2139 AM, Al5X1, AlF357), SLM Solutions / Nikon SLM, 3D Systems (A6061-RAM2 licence), Colibrium / GE Additive, Mercury Marine (Mercalloy A362 for AM), Gränges (Dispal-type Al-Si-Fe-Ni), PEAK Werkstoff / Erbslöh (Dispal S220/S250 Al-Si), Kaiser, Novelis, Uniformity Labs.
16. Any patents specifically on aluminium powders made by ULTRASONIC atomization or small-batch atomization for alloy development.

Then answer:
A. Which claimed composition windows overlap a search space of Al >= 85 wt% with a few additions from Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn? Where is there apparent white space (combinations nobody has claimed or published), especially Sc-free and with little or no Zr?
B. Which commercial Sc-free alloys have the highest reported yield strength at >= 8 % elongation, and what do their datasheets give for as-built versus heat-treated?
C. Which patent example compositions would make good seed experiments for us, given feedstock on hand (Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, small Sc and Er; Fe, Cu and Ni easy to buy; Zr uncertain)?
D. Anything in these patents about atomization practice (melt temperature, superheat for Zr/Ti/Cr/Mn-bearing melts, crucible materials, Mg loss) or about build-plate preheat that we should copy.

Give patent numbers and URLs or DOIs for every claim. Say clearly when a composition comes from a datasheet, a patent example, a patent claim range, or a journal paper by the same group.
task_summary: Survey Patent And Commercial Aluminium Alloys For LPBF Compile Compositions Claims Properties And Recommendations

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: open_targets_search

Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal

    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions

        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation

    InterventionalAssignment:

    ObservationalModel:

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

filter for minimum publication year.

filter for maximum publication year.

max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)

Use the tools to answer the question: Survey the PATENT literature and COMMERCIAL products for aluminium alloys designed for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) and related powder routes, so that we can choose starting compositions for an alloy discovery campaign and know what is already claimed. We want published compositions, not marketing.

For each entry give: assignee / vendor, product name if any, patent or application numbers (US, EP, WO, CN, JP, DE), priority year, the claimed composition RANGES and the worked EXAMPLE compositions (wt%), the cracking-control and strengthening mechanism claimed, recommended heat treatment, the properties reported in the patent or datasheet (yield, UTS, elongation, hardness, conductivity, test orientation), and whether the patent is granted, pending, expired or abandoned where known.

Cover at least:
1. Airbus / APWorks Scalmalloy (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr-Mn), and the earlier Al-Mg-Sc family patents; lower-Sc or Sc-free variants claimed by others.
2. HRL Laboratories 7A77 and Zr / grain-refiner functionalized 7xxx, 6xxx, 2xxx powders.
3. Aeromet / Aluminium Materials Technologies A20X (A205; Al-Cu-Ag-Mg-Ti-B).
4. NanoAl / Unity Aluminum / Braidy Addalloy (Al-Mg-Zr and others) and Northwestern University Al-Zr-(Er, Sc, Yb, Si) patents.
5. Constellium Aheadd CP1 (Al-Fe-Zr) and HT1 (Al-Ni-Mn-Cu-Zr-Fe class), and the C-TEC patent families (Al-Zr, Al-Fe-Zr, Al-Ni-Zr, Al-Mn-Zr, Al-Cr-Zr).
6. Fehrmann AlMgty (Al-Mg-Si / high-Mg), Rheinfelden (Magsimal, Castasil, Castaduct for AM), AMAG, Hydro, Trimet.
7. Elementum 3D A1000-RAM, A2024-RAM2, A6061-RAM2, A7050-RAM2 (reactive additive manufacturing, in-situ ceramic inoculants).
8. Rusal / IL&M (RS-230, RS-300, RS-320, RS-333, RS-390, RS-553 and similar: Al-Si-Mg-Cu, Al-Mg-Sc, Al-Ni-Mn-Fe-Zr, Al-Cu-Ce), with compositions.
9. Monash University / Amaero high-strength Al-Mn-Sc ("HOT Al"), and Al-Mg-Si-Sc-Zr.
10. Chalmers / Hoganas Al-Mn-Cr-Zr; Hoganas forAM Al grades; Kymera / ECKA / AP&C / Equispheres / Valimet / Carpenter / Sandvik / Toyal / Eckart (e.g. Eckart TiB2- or Zr-modified, Toyal Hyper-Al) aluminium AM powders with published chemistries.
11. Oak Ridge / Eck Industries / Ames Al-Ce alloys (Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Ce-Ni-Mn, Al-Cu-Mn-Zr / ACMZ, DuAlumin-3D), Lawrence Livermore Al-Ce.
12. Alcoa / Arconic / Howmet AM aluminium (Al-Fe-V-Si, Al-Ni, Al-Mn, "A1000" class), QuesTek Al for AM (Sc-free, high-temperature), Citrine / HRL / NASA collaborations, NASA 7xxx / GRCop is out of scope.
13. Japanese and Korean filings: Toyo Aluminium, Daido, Kobe Steel, UACJ, Nippon Light Metal, Sumitomo, Hitachi Metals, Toyota (Al-Fe, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Ni-Co, Al-Mn-Cr, Al-Si-Mg-Mn high-Mg).
14. Chinese filings and products: CRRC / Central South University Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, Al-Mg-Er-Zr (Beijing University of Technology Er-microalloying patents), Al-Mn-Mg-Er-Zr, TiB2/AlSi10Mg (Shanghai Jiao Tong), Al-Zn-Mg-Sc-Zr, Sc-free high-strength Al for AM.
15. EOS (Al2139 AM, Al5X1, AlF357), SLM Solutions / Nikon SLM, 3D Systems (A6061-RAM2 licence), Colibrium / GE Additive, Mercury Marine (Mercalloy A362 for AM), Gränges (Dispal-type Al-Si-Fe-Ni), PEAK Werkstoff / Erbslöh (Dispal S220/S250 Al-Si), Kaiser, Novelis, Uniformity Labs.
16. Any patents specifically on aluminium powders made by ULTRASONIC atomization or small-batch atomization for alloy development.

Then answer:
A. Which claimed composition windows overlap a search space of Al >= 85 wt% with a few additions from Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn? Where is there apparent white space (combinations nobody has claimed or published), especially Sc-free and with little or no Zr?
B. Which commercial Sc-free alloys have the highest reported yield strength at >= 8 % elongation, and what do their datasheets give for as-built versus heat-treated?
C. Which patent example compositions would make good seed experiments for us, given feedstock on hand (Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, small Sc and Er; Fe, Cu and Ni easy to buy; Zr uncertain)?
D. Anything in these patents about atomization practice (melt temperature, superheat for Zr/Ti/Cr/Mn-bearing melts, crucible materials, Mg loss) or about build-plate preheat that we should copy.

Give patent numbers and URLs or DOIs for every claim. Say clearly when a composition comes from a datasheet, a patent example, a patent claim range, or a journal paper by the same group.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to survey the patent and commercial landscape for aluminum alloys designed for LPBF/SLM. This is an extensive research task that I'll break into systematic phases.

    author = "Aversa, Alberta and Marchese, Giulio and Saboori, Abdollah and Bassini, Emilio and Manfredi, Diego and Biamino, Sara and Ugues, Daniele and Fino, Paolo and Lombardi, Mariangela",
    title = "New Aluminum Alloys Specifically Designed for Laser Powder Bed Fusion: A Review",

    volume = "12",
    pages = "1007",
    month = "Mar",

    issue = "7",
    issn = "1996-1944"
}


Abstract:
Aluminum alloys are key materials in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies thanks to their low density that, coupled with the possibility to create complex geometries of these innovative processes, can be exploited for several applications in aerospace and automotive fields. The AM process of these alloys had to face many challenges because, due to their low laser absorption, high thermal conductivity and reduced powder flowability, they are characterized by poor processability. Nowadays mainly Al-Si alloys are processed, however, in recent years many efforts have been carried out in developing new compositions specifically designed for laser based powder bed AM processes. Abstract:
Scalmalloy® is an Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy designed for the additive manufacturing of components used in various industrial applications. It is primarily used in aerospace and automotive fields due to its low density and high strength. The present brief review aims to outline the state-of-the-art heat treatments currently applied on the as-built Scalmalloy®. The as-built alloy shows yield strength values of 256–278 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 349–350 MPa, and elongation of 19.0–20.0% due to its bimodal microstructure, which is formed by fine and coarse grain zones. These microstructural features lead to an isotropic behaviour of the mechanical properties. Varying the process parameters, yield strength and ultimate tensile strength can reach values higher than 300 MPa and 400 MPa, respectively, maintaining an isotropic behaviour. After direct aging heat treatment (325 °C × 4 h), the yield and ultimate tensile strength values increase up to 456–469 MPa and 512–521 MPa, respectively, while the strain decreases to 12.0–13.0% due to phase precipitation in the α-Al matrix. Notably, the bimodal microstructure remains largely unchanged. The HIP treatment, carried out at 325 °C × 4 h with a pressure of 1000 bar, reduced the porosity (approximatively 0.18%), resulting in further improvements. The yield strength and the ultimate tensile strength rose to 482–493 MPa and 523–547 MPa, respectively.

Abstract:
This study shows a rapid and systematic approach towards identifying full density and peak hardness for an Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy commonly known as Scalmalloy®. The alloy is tailored for the laser powder bed fusion process and has been shown to be printable with >99.8% relative density. The microstructure suggests Al grain refinement in melt pool boundaries, associated with formation of primary Al3(Sc,Zr) particles during solidification. Peak hardening response was identified by heat treatment tests at 573,598 and 623 K between 0 and 10 h. A peak hardness of 172 HV0.3 at 598 K for 4 h was identified. The mechanical properties were also tested with yield and ultimate strengths of 287 MPa and 364 MPa in as-printed and 468 MPa and 517 MPa in peak hardened conditions, respectively, which is consistent with the literature. Such an approach is considered apt when qualifying new materials in industrial laser powder bed fusion systems. The second part of the study discusses the thermal stability of such alloys post-peak-hardening. One set of samples was peak hardened at the conditions identified before and underwent secondary ageing at three different temperatures of 423,473 and 523 K between 0 and 120 h to understand thermal stability and benchmark against conventional Al alloys. The secondary heat treatments performed at lower temperatures revealed lower deterioration of hardness over ageing times as compared to the datasheets for conventional Al alloys and Scalmalloy®, thus suggesting that longer ageing times are needed.

Abstract:
In this study, the correlation between the microstructure and tribological performance of Sc and Zr-modified Al–Mg alloy (Scalmalloy®) samples produced via laser powder bed fusion process was evaluated via a dry sliding Pin-on-Disc wear test under different planes, directions, and various normal applied loads. The results revealed a remarkable dependency of wear properties on the as-built microstructure so that different behaviors were observed along the scanning and building planes. The microstructural examination indicated the presence of bi-modal grains and finely shaped equiaxed grains observed in the building and scanning planes, respectively. Increasing the applied loads from 20 to 40 N led to a significant increase in the coefficient of friction (COF) while increasing the load from 40 to 60 N, slightly decreasing the COF for the studied samples. No dependency was found between the COF and the corresponding microstructure at the highest applied load. The anisotropic wear resistance and COF values were predominant at the lowest applied load. Due to tailored as-built microstructural features and different microhardness values, lower wear rates were noticed along the scanning plane for all applied loads. Under the 20 N applied load, however, the worn surface of the scanning plane showed a clearer and smoother surface compared to the building plane surfaces. Ultra-fine equiaxed grains along the scanning plane and columnar grains along the building plane were determined as the main factors creating anisotropic tribological behavior. The outcomes of this study can pave the way toward producing more wear-resistant surfaces and developing components for critical wear applications in as-built conditions with no need for expensive and time-consuming surface treatments.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)-manufactured Sc-Zr-modified Al–Mg alloy (Scalmalloy) has a bimodal microstructure comprising coarse grains (CGs) in the hot melt pool area and ultrafine grains (UFGs) along the melt pool boundaries (MPBs). Owing to these microstructural features, an increase in the MPBs can increase the UFGs, leading to enhanced mechanical properties. However, the effects of the LPBF process parameters, especially the laser scan strategy, on the microstructure and mechanical properties of Scalmalloy are still unclear. Here, a comparative study was conducted between X- and XY-mode laser scan strategies, with the same volumetric energy, based on the melt pool configuration, grain size distribution, and precipitation behaviors. The X-scan exhibited mechanical properties superior to those exhibited by the XY-scan, attributed to the higher volume fraction (VF) of UFGs. An increase in the VF of UFGs was observed, from 46% for the XY-scan to 56% for the X-scan, owing to an increase in MPBs. Consequently, the tensile strength of the X-scan was higher than that of the XY-scan. The maximum yield strength (271.5 ± 2.7 MPa) was obtained for the X-scan strategy, which was approximately twice that obtained for casting. The results of this study demonstrate that the microstructure and mechanical properties of Scalmalloy can be successfully tuned by a laser scanning strategy.

Abstract:
This paper reviews the status of nanoparticle technology as it relates to the additive manufacturing (AM) of aluminum-based alloys. A broad overview of common AM processes is given. Additive manufacturing is a promising field for the advancement of manufacturing due to its ability to yield near-net-shaped components that require minimal post-processing prior to end-use. AM also allows for the fabrication of prototypes as well as economical small batch production. Aluminum alloys processed via AM would be very beneficial to the manufacturing industry due to their high strength to weight ratio; however, many of the conventional alloy compositions have been shown to be incompatible with AM processing methods. As a result, many investigations have looked to methods to improve the processability of these alloys. This paper explores the use of nanostructures to enhance the processability of aluminum alloys. It is concluded that the addition of nanostructures is a promising route for modification of existing alloys and may be beneficial to other powder-based processes.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
          <jats:p>The integration of machine learning (ML) into alloy design has revolutionized the discovery and optimization of advanced materials by enabling high-throughput, data-driven methodologies. This review systematically examines recent advancements in ML applications across diverse alloy systems, including steels, aluminum alloys, magnesium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), shape memory alloys, and metallic glasses. We categorize ML approaches into supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning paradigms, detailing their specific implementations for property prediction, phase stability analysis, and composition optimization. Advanced techniques, such as inverse design frameworks and physics-informed ML models, have demonstrated substantial improvements in predictive accuracy and interpretability by integrating domain knowledge with data-driven approaches. The review further explores the synergy between ML and traditional computational methods, including CALPHAD-based thermodynamic modeling and density functional theory (DFT), enhancing the reliability of property predictions. We highlight case studies where ML-driven strategies have successfully accelerated alloy discovery, optimized mechanical properties, and identified novel compositions with tailored performance metrics. Additionally, we address key challenges in ML-driven alloy design, including data scarcity, feature selection, model interpretability, and the necessity for standardized benchmarking datasets. By providing a comprehensive evaluation of current methodologies and emerging trends, this review underscores the transformative role of ML in advancing next-generation alloy design and manufacturing, ultimately enabling the rapid development of high-performance materials for aerospace, energy, biomedical, and structural applications.</jats:p>

CA3162961C, titled “Heat-resistant aluminium powder material,” describes a Rusal Engineering and Technological Center/Tianjin University aluminium alloy powder for additive manufacturing. The claimed composition is, in wt.%: Ni 2.5–5.5, Mn 1.0–3.5, Fe 0.15–2.0, Zr 0.2–1.0, and Ce 0.05–0.4. It additionally contains 0.05–1.5 wt.% total of one or more of Cu, Mg, and Zn, plus 0.1–2.0 wt.% total of one or more of Si and Ca; aluminium and unavoidable impurities make up the balance. Nickel, manganese, and iron must satisfy Ni > Mn + Fe. The alloy is intended to form thermally stable eutectic phases, including Al3Ni, Al16Mn3Ni, and Al9FeNi, together with Al3Zr-type dispersoids. The claimed tensile strength is at least 370 MPa after printing or stress-relief annealing. Claimed powder size ranges are 10–150 µm and 10–63 µm, and production may use nitrogen or argon gas atomization, optionally with 0.1–0.8 wt.% oxygen. Products may be manufactured by additive technologies, with one claim specifying solidification rates of at least 1000 K/s. DEFINITIONS

the present invention
       generally relates to processes for additive manufacturing using optimized metal-
       containing precursors (e.g., powders).
Metal-based additive manufacturing
       has applications in many industries, including the aerospace and automotive industries.
       Building up metal components layer-by-layer increases design freedom and
       manufacturing ﬂexibility, thereby enabling complex geometries while eliminating
        traditional economy-of-scale constraints.
a direct energy source

to melt alloy powders
        locally results in solidiﬁcation rates between 0.1 m/s and 5 m/s, an order of magnitude
       increase over conventional casting processes.
Additive manufacturing
       allows for one-step fabrication of complex parts of arbitrary design. Additive
       manufacturing eliminates the need for assembling multiple components or setting up
     new equipment, while minimizing manufacturing time and wastage of materials and
       energy. Although additive manufacturing is rapidly growing to produce metallic,
       polymeric, and ceramic components, production of metallic parts is its fastest growing
        sector.the only printable aluminum alloys
       are based on the binary Al—Si system and tend to converge around a yield strength of
       approximately 200 MPa with a low ductility of 4%.
the exception
          is Scalmalloy, which relies on alloying additions of scandium, a rare high-cost metal.
most aluminum alloys used in automotive, aerospace, and consumer applications
       are wrought alloys of the 2000, 5000, 6000, or 7000 series, which can exhibit strengths
       exceeding 400 MPa and ductility of more than 10% but cannot currently be additively
       manufactured.
These systems
      have low-cost alloying elements (Cu, Mg, Zn, and Si) carefully selected to produce
      complex strengthening phases during subsequent ageing. These same elements promote
        large solidiﬁcation ranges, leading to hot tearing (cracking) during solidiﬁcation—a
      problem that has been diﬃcult to surmount for more than 100 years since the ﬁrst age-
       hardenable alloy, duralumin, was developed.
the primary equilibrium phase
        solidiﬁes ﬁrst at a diﬀerent composition from the bulk liquid.
This mechanism
        results in solute enrichment in the liquid near the solidifying interface, locally changing
       the equilibrium liquidus temperature and producing an unstable, undercooled condition.
there is a breakdown of the solid—liquid interface
       leading to cellular or dendritic grain growth with long channels of interdendritic liquid
       trapped between solidiﬁed regions.
volumetric solidiﬁcation shrinkage and thermal contraction in these channels
       produces cavities and hot tearing cracks which may span the entire length of the
      columnar grain and can propagate through additional intergranular regions.
aluminum alloys Al 7075 and Al 6061
       are highly susceptible to the formation of such cracks, due to a lack of processing paths
        to produce ﬁne equiaxed grains.
a reduction in peak temperature and a smaller surface-to-volume ratio of the melt pool
     may minimize pronounced changes of chemical composition during laser processing.
      However, it is not always possible to minimize temperature due to the presence of high-
       melting-point metals that need to be liqueﬁed during additive manufacturing. Likewise,

## pqac-00000048

From text 'US20210254196A1 pages 11-12'.

Joseph R. Croteau. High-performance al-zn-mg-zr base aluminum alloys for welding and additive …. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP,KR), 2021.

The excerpt identifies an Al-Zn-Mg-Zr alloy system in which magnesium is present at about 0.3–2 wt.%, zirconium at about 0.3–2 wt.%, and copper, when used, at up to about 3 wt.%; aluminum makes up the balance. The composition is described as free of intentionally added scandium. Examples include Al-11Zn-2.5Mg-1Cu and the Zr-containing Al-11Zn-2.5Mg-1Cu-1.5Zr composition. Additional comparison examples are Al-10Zn-3Mg, Al-10Zn-3Mg-1.2Zr, and Al-10Zn-3Mg-(0.6–1.2)Zr. The reported benefits of Zr include grain refinement, preservation of a refined microstructure after processing, hardening during solutionizing through Al3Zr nanoprecipitation, improved thermal stability, and resistance to high-temperature grain growth. These characteristics are relevant to welding and additive manufacturing because conventional 7000-series alloys can experience grain growth, segregation, hot cracking, and reduced weld strength. The excerpt does not provide numerical tensile, yield-strength, elongation, hardness, or other quantitative mechanical-property values. It states qualitatively that conventional weld fusion zones often have much lower strength than the base material, while the disclosed Zr-containing alloys are intended to improve microstructural stability and weldability.

## pqac-00000050

From text 'US10941473B2 pages 21-22'.

David R. Snyder. Aluminum alloys. Patent (WO,EP,US,JP), 2021.

The excerpt is from Snyder, US10,941,473B2, rather than the cited Croteau US20210254196A1, but it provides closely relevant Al-Zn-Mg-Zr alloy information for welding and additive manufacturing. The disclosed composition range is approximately 3–9 wt% Zn, 2–6 wt% Mg, 0.5–2 wt% Cu, and 0–1 wt% Zr, with optional Y, Er, Yb, Sc, Ag, and Mn, balance aluminum. Examples include approximately 6.3 Zn–3.5 Mg–1.1 Cu–0.1 Zr and 7.5 Zn–4.6 Mg–1.5 Cu–0.1 Zr; the table also lists alloys containing roughly 3.3–3.0 Zn, 4.7–5.5 Mg, 1.3–1.4 Cu, and 0.1 Zr. Bead-on-plate welding trials reported elimination of hot cracking for Alloys 1–3, unlike 6061 and 7050. T7 hardness values were 183, 184, 168, and 165 Vickers for Alloys 1–4, respectively, compared with 105 for AlSi10Mg-T6, 124 for 6061-T6, and 172 for 7050-T7. Alloy 4 was successfully gas-atomized and DMLS-processed; suitable parameters produced crack-free, dense builds with below 0.5% porosity and approximately 10 µm average pore size.

## pqac-00000051

From text 'US11603583B2 pages 1-4'.

Nhon Q. Vo. Ribbons and powders from high strength corrosion resistant aluminum alloys. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP), 2023.

The excerpt does not identify US20210254196A1 (Croteau et al.) specifically and does not provide a Zn-containing Al-Zn-Mg-Zr composition range or numerical mechanical-property data. It instead describes a related rapid-solidification aluminum alloy family based on magnesium and zirconium, with aluminum as the balance: 1–10 wt.% Mg and 0.3–3 wt.% Zr, preferably 0.45–3 wt.% Zr. Vanadium may optionally be present at 0.3–1.5 wt.%. The alloys are stated to be free of intentionally added scandium, with any impurity limited to 0.05 wt.%. Example compositions include Al-3.6Mg-1.2Zr wt.% powder used for 3D-printed components, Al-4Mg-1.7Zr wt.% melt-spun alloy, and an at.% example identified as Al-4.5Mg-0.5Zr. The materials are intended for additive manufacturing, spray deposition, compaction, ribbons, and powders, and are described as weldable. Reported mechanical characteristics are qualitative rather than numerical: high strength and ductility, high creep resistance, excellent corrosion resistance, and strength retention at elevated temperatures. Al3Zr primary precipitates and nanoscale Al3Zr precipitates provide dispersion/precipitation strengthening and remain stable up to approximately 425°C; some embodiments are heat- and creep-resistant to 400°C.

The alloy contains uniformly distributed α-Al(Mn,Fe)Si precipitates, with peak-aged number densities above about 10^22 m−3 and mean radii below about 25 nm. It also forms Al-X nanoprecipitates, where X is Sn, In, Sb, or Bi, with an approximately 1.5 nm mean radius. A claimed peak microhardness is approximately 525±5 MPa after aging to about 475°C. The abstract describes cubic α-Al(Mn,TM)Si precipitates, approximately 25 nm in mean radius and about 2% volume fraction, and emphasizes high-temperature strength, creep and coarsening resistance.

messages.content: Now let me create the main summary table artifact and then proceed to the analysis:

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive table of aluminum alloys designed for LPBF/SLM with the following columns: Family/Product Name, Assignee/Vendor, Patent/Application Numbers, Priority Year, Alloy System, Claimed Composition Ranges (wt%), Worked Example Compositions (wt%), Cracking-Control / Strengthening Mechanism, Recommended Heat Treatment, Properties (YS / UTS / El% / Hardness), Status (Granted/Pending/Expired). Include the following entries based on the evidence gathered:

1. Scalmalloy (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr-Mn): Airbus/APWorks, patent EP2766136B1 (priority 2011), WO2008/125092 (priority 2007). Claimed: Mg 0.5-10, Sc 0.2-2.0, Zr 0.2-2.0, Mn 0-1.0. Preferred: Mg 2.5-5.0, Sc 0.3-1.0, Zr 0.2-0.5, Mn 0.1-0.8. Worked: Al-4.4Mg-0.8Sc-0.3Zr-0.5Mn. Mechanism: Al3(Sc,Zr) grain refinement + precipitation. Heat treatment: 325°C/4h aging. As-built: YS 256-278, UTS 349-350, El 19-20%. Aged: YS 456-469, UTS 512-521, El 12-13%. Granted.

2. Scancromal: Airbus, US20220186346A1. Al-Cr-Sc-Zr. Worked: Al-2.6Cr-0.7Sc-0.3Zr. High compressive strength. Pending.

3. Scantital: Airbus, US20220168811A1. Ti 0.1-15, Sc 0.1-3.0, Zr 0.1-3.0. Worked: Al-1.0Ti-1.0Sc-0.4Zr. Pending.

4. HRL 7075+Zr: HRL Labs, US11919085B2 (priority 2015), US11053571B2, US11286543B2. Base 7075 + ~1 vol% ZrH2 nanoparticles. Mechanism: ZrH2→Al3Zr grain refinement. T6: 480°C/2h + 120°C/18h. Crack-free equiaxed. Granted.

5. HRL 7A77-type: HRL Labs, US11578389B2 (priority 2017). Feedstock: Al 79.8-88.3, Cu 1.1-2.1, Mg 3.0-4.6, Zn 7.1-9.0, Zr 0.5-2.8. As-built target: Al 84.5-92.1, Cu 1.1-2.1, Mg 1.8-2.9, Zn 4.5-6.1, Zr 0.5-2.8. Mechanism: Zr grain refinement + enriched Mg/Zn feedstock to compensate vaporization loss (~25% Zn, ~30% Mg). Granted.

6. NanoAl/Braidy Addalloy: NanoAl/Unity, US11603583B2 (Vo, priority ~2017). Al-1-10Mg-0.3-3Zr, Sc-free. Al3Zr L12 dispersoids. Granted.

7. NanoAl 7xxx-type: Snyder, US10941473B2 (priority ~2018). Zn 3-9, Mg 2-6, Cu 0.5-2, Zr 0-1, optional Er/Yb/Sc. Examples: Al-6.3Zn-3.5Mg-1.1Cu-0.1Zr. Eutectic-based cracking control. Hardness ~183 HV. Granted.

8. Northwestern Al-Zn-Mg-Zr: Croteau, US20210254196A1 (priority ~2019). Zn 4-12, Mg 1-4, Zr 0.3-2, optional Cu to 3. Example: Al-11Zn-2.5Mg-1Cu-1.5Zr. Al3Zr grain refinement. Pending.

9. MIT/Mousavi Al-Zr-Er: US20260002237A1 (priority ~2023). Al >80 mol%, Zr 0.1-1.5, Er 0.1-1 mol%, optional Ni to 2 mol%. L12 Al3(Zr,Er). YS ≥400 MPa. Pending.

10. Constellium Aheadd CP1-type: WO2020095009A2 (Chehab, priority 2018). Zr 0.5-2.5, Fe 0-3, Mg ≤0.2, Cu 0.05-0.5. No solution treatment needed. Focus on conductivity. Pending/families granted.

11. Constellium broader C-TEC: EP3914748B1, EP4149702A2. Broader Al-Fe-Zr and Al-Ni-Mn families. Granted/Pending.

12. Rusal RS-553 type: CA3162961C (Mann, priority ~2019). Ni 2.5-5.5, Mn 1.0-3.5, Fe 0.15-2.0, Zr 0.2-1.0, Ce 0.05-0.4, Cu/Mg/Zn 0.05-1.5 total, Si/Ca 0.1-2.0. Ni > Mn+Fe. Example: Al-1.9Mn-3.6Ni-0.7Fe-0.2Ce-0.28Zr-0.3Cu-0.2Mg. UTS 442, YS 325, El 5.3%. Heat resistant to 300°C. Granted.

13. Monash/Amaero HOT Al: US11976343B2 (Rometsch, priority 2017). Mn 2.01-15, Sc 0.3-2.0, optional Mg 0-6, Zr 0-4. Worked: Al-4.52Mn-1.32Mg-0.79Sc-0.74Zr. As-built YS 427, UTS 453, El 12.0%. Aged 300°C/5h: YS 577, UTS 588, El 11.3%. Direct aging only. Granted.

14. Alcoa Al-Fe-V-Si-Cu: US20160138400A1 (Karabin, priority ~2014). Fe 3-12, V 0.1-3, Si 0.1-3, Cu 1-6. Example: Al-8.14Fe-1.48V-1.66Si-2.10Cu. AlFeVSi dispersoids. Aging 125-200°C. Pending.

15. Oak Ridge/Eck Al-Ce: WO2018052517A9 (Weiss, priority 2016). Ce (or RE) 4-20 wt%, optional Mg to 15, Si to 12, Fe to 6, Ni to 8, Cu to 8. Examples: Al-8Ce-10Mg, Al-12Ce-4Si-0.4Mg. Stable eutectic, coarsening-resistant. Al-12Ce-4Si-0.4Mg T6: UTS 252 MPa. Pending/Granted.

16. ORNL Al-Ce: US12305267B2 (Rios, priority ~2017). RE 5-30, Mg 0.4-12. Examples: Al-8Ce-0.4Mg, Al-12Ce-0.4Mg, Al-8Ce-8Mg. Granted.

17. Beijing Univ. Tech. Al-Mg-Er-Zr: Journal paper Guo 2022. Al-6Mg-0.7Mn-0.4Er-1.2Zr. Sc-free. As-built: YS 325, UTS 438, El 18%. Aged 375°C/10h: UTS 520, El 15.5%. Al3(Er,Zr) core-shell. Paper.

18. Farkoosh Al-Mn-Si-Sn: US12104237B2 (priority ~2020). Mn 0.3-0.7 at%, Si 0.2-1.0 at%, Sn 0.01-0.02 at%. α-Al(Mn,Fe)Si precipitates. Microhardness 525-725 MPa. Granted."}

messages.content: Now let me create the white-space analysis and recommendations artifact:

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table analyzing white space and seed composition recommendations for the user's alloy discovery campaign. The table should address Questions A-D from the user's request.

Section A - White Space Analysis: Create rows for different element combinations showing whether they overlap with known patent claims or represent white space. Focus on combinations from {Al >= 85 wt%, Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn}. Key white space areas to highlight (Sc-free and little/no Zr):

1. Al-Mn-Cr-Si (no Sc, no Zr) - Largely unclaimed for LPBF except Farkoosh Al-Mn-Si-Sn
2. Al-Mn-Mg-Cr (no Sc, no Zr) - Not covered by specific claims when Cr > 0.5 and no Sc
3. Al-Mg-Mn-Si-Sn (no Sc, no Zr) - Partly overlaps Farkoosh at low Mn
4. Al-Mn-Cr-Fe-Si (no Sc, no Zr, no RE) - Open space
5. Al-Cu-Mn-Cr-Mg (no Sc, no Zr) - Not covered
6. Al-Mg-Mn-Ni (no Sc, low/no Zr) - Partially overlaps Rusal if Ni > 2.5
7. Al-Mg-Si-Cr-Ti (no Sc, no Zr) - Open

Areas well-claimed:
- Al-Mg-Sc-Zr: Scalmalloy family
- Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr: HRL, Snyder, Croteau
- Al-Fe-Zr: Constellium
- Al-Ni-Mn-Fe-Zr: Rusal
- Al-Mn-Sc: Monash/Amaero
- Al-Mg-Zr (Sc-free): NanoAl

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,

- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions

        - DEVICE: Device interventions

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Survey the PATENT literature and COMMERCIAL products for aluminium alloys designed for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) and related powder routes, so that we can choose starting compositions for an alloy discovery campaign and know what is already claimed. We want published compositions, not marketing.

For each entry give: assignee / vendor, product name if any, patent or application numbers (US, EP, WO, CN, JP, DE), priority year, the claimed composition RANGES and the worked EXAMPLE compositions (wt%), the cracking-control and strengthening mechanism claimed, recommended heat treatment, the properties reported in the patent or datasheet (yield, UTS, elongation, hardness, conductivity, test orientation), and whether the patent is granted, pending, expired or abandoned where known.

Cover at least:
1. Airbus / APWorks Scalmalloy (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr-Mn), and the earlier Al-Mg-Sc family patents; lower-Sc or Sc-free variants claimed by others.
2. HRL Laboratories 7A77 and Zr / grain-refiner functionalized 7xxx, 6xxx, 2xxx powders.
3. Aeromet / Aluminium Materials Technologies A20X (A205; Al-Cu-Ag-Mg-Ti-B).
4. NanoAl / Unity Aluminum / Braidy Addalloy (Al-Mg-Zr and others) and Northwestern University Al-Zr-(Er, Sc, Yb, Si) patents.

Abstract:
Aluminum alloys are key materials in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies thanks to their low density that, coupled with the possibility to create complex geometries of these innovative processes, can be exploited for several applications in aerospace and automotive fields. The AM process of these alloys had to face many challenges because, due to their low laser absorption, high thermal conductivity and reduced powder flowability, they are characterized by poor processability. Nowadays mainly Al-Si alloys are processed, however, in recent years many efforts have been carried out in developing new compositions specifically designed for laser based powder bed AM processes. This paper reviews the state of the art of the aluminum alloys used in the laser powder bed fusion process, together with the microstructural and mechanical characterizations.
