Abstract:
Scalmalloy® is an Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy designed for the additive manufacturing of components used in various industrial applications. It is primarily used in aerospace and automotive fields due to its low density and high strength. The present brief review aims to outline the state-of-the-art heat treatments currently applied on the as-built Scalmalloy®. The as-built alloy shows yield strength values of 256–278 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 349–350 MPa, and elongation of 19.0–20.0% due to its bimodal microstructure, which is formed by fine and coarse grain zones. These microstructural features lead to an isotropic behaviour of the mechanical properties. Varying the process parameters, yield strength and ultimate tensile strength can reach values higher than 300 MPa and 400 MPa, respectively, maintaining an isotropic behaviour. After direct aging heat treatment (325 °C × 4 h), the yield and ultimate tensile strength values increase up to 456–469 MPa and 512–521 MPa, respectively, while the strain decreases to 12.0–13.0% due to phase precipitation in the α-Al matrix. Notably, the bimodal microstructure remains largely unchanged. The HIP treatment, carried out at 325 °C × 4 h with a pressure of 1000 bar, reduced the porosity (approximatively 0.18%), resulting in further improvements. The yield strength and the ultimate tensile strength rose to 482–493 MPa and 523–547 MPa, respectively.

Abstract:
This study shows a rapid and systematic approach towards identifying full density and peak hardness for an Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy commonly known as Scalmalloy®. The alloy is tailored for the laser powder bed fusion process and has been shown to be printable with >99.8% relative density. The microstructure suggests Al grain refinement in melt pool boundaries, associated with formation of primary Al3(Sc,Zr) particles during solidification. Peak hardening response was identified by heat treatment tests at 573,598 and 623 K between 0 and 10 h. A peak hardness of 172 HV0.3 at 598 K for 4 h was identified. The mechanical properties were also tested with yield and ultimate strengths of 287 MPa and 364 MPa in as-printed and 468 MPa and 517 MPa in peak hardened conditions, respectively, which is consistent with the literature. Such an approach is considered apt when qualifying new materials in industrial laser powder bed fusion systems. The second part of the study discusses the thermal stability of such alloys post-peak-hardening. One set of samples was peak hardened at the conditions identified before and underwent secondary ageing at three different temperatures of 423,473 and 523 K between 0 and 120 h to understand thermal stability and benchmark against conventional Al alloys. The secondary heat treatments performed at lower temperatures revealed lower deterioration of hardness over ageing times as compared to the datasheets for conventional Al alloys and Scalmalloy®, thus suggesting that longer ageing times are needed.

Abstract:
In this study, the correlation between the microstructure and tribological performance of Sc and Zr-modified Al–Mg alloy (Scalmalloy®) samples produced via laser powder bed fusion process was evaluated via a dry sliding Pin-on-Disc wear test under different planes, directions, and various normal applied loads. The results revealed a remarkable dependency of wear properties on the as-built microstructure so that different behaviors were observed along the scanning and building planes. The microstructural examination indicated the presence of bi-modal grains and finely shaped equiaxed grains observed in the building and scanning planes, respectively. Increasing the applied loads from 20 to 40 N led to a significant increase in the coefficient of friction (COF) while increasing the load from 40 to 60 N, slightly decreasing the COF for the studied samples. No dependency was found between the COF and the corresponding microstructure at the highest applied load. The anisotropic wear resistance and COF values were predominant at the lowest applied load. Due to tailored as-built microstructural features and different microhardness values, lower wear rates were noticed along the scanning plane for all applied loads. Under the 20 N applied load, however, the worn surface of the scanning plane showed a clearer and smoother surface compared to the building plane surfaces. Ultra-fine equiaxed grains along the scanning plane and columnar grains along the building plane were determined as the main factors creating anisotropic tribological behavior. The outcomes of this study can pave the way toward producing more wear-resistant surfaces and developing components for critical wear applications in as-built conditions with no need for expensive and time-consuming surface treatments.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)-manufactured Sc-Zr-modified Al–Mg alloy (Scalmalloy) has a bimodal microstructure comprising coarse grains (CGs) in the hot melt pool area and ultrafine grains (UFGs) along the melt pool boundaries (MPBs). Owing to these microstructural features, an increase in the MPBs can increase the UFGs, leading to enhanced mechanical properties. However, the effects of the LPBF process parameters, especially the laser scan strategy, on the microstructure and mechanical properties of Scalmalloy are still unclear. Here, a comparative study was conducted between X- and XY-mode laser scan strategies, with the same volumetric energy, based on the melt pool configuration, grain size distribution, and precipitation behaviors. The X-scan exhibited mechanical properties superior to those exhibited by the XY-scan, attributed to the higher volume fraction (VF) of UFGs. An increase in the VF of UFGs was observed, from 46% for the XY-scan to 56% for the X-scan, owing to an increase in MPBs. Consequently, the tensile strength of the X-scan was higher than that of the XY-scan. The maximum yield strength (271.5 ± 2.7 MPa) was obtained for the X-scan strategy, which was approximately twice that obtained for casting. The results of this study demonstrate that the microstructure and mechanical properties of Scalmalloy can be successfully tuned by a laser scanning strategy.

Abstract:
This paper reviews the status of nanoparticle technology as it relates to the additive manufacturing (AM) of aluminum-based alloys. A broad overview of common AM processes is given. Additive manufacturing is a promising field for the advancement of manufacturing due to its ability to yield near-net-shaped components that require minimal post-processing prior to end-use. AM also allows for the fabrication of prototypes as well as economical small batch production. Aluminum alloys processed via AM would be very beneficial to the manufacturing industry due to their high strength to weight ratio; however, many of the conventional alloy compositions have been shown to be incompatible with AM processing methods. As a result, many investigations have looked to methods to improve the processability of these alloys. This paper explores the use of nanostructures to enhance the processability of aluminum alloys. It is concluded that the addition of nanostructures is a promising route for modification of existing alloys and may be beneficial to other powder-based processes.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
          <jats:p>The integration of machine learning (ML) into alloy design has revolutionized the discovery and optimization of advanced materials by enabling high-throughput, data-driven methodologies. This review systematically examines recent advancements in ML applications across diverse alloy systems, including steels, aluminum alloys, magnesium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), shape memory alloys, and metallic glasses. We categorize ML approaches into supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning paradigms, detailing their specific implementations for property prediction, phase stability analysis, and composition optimization. Advanced techniques, such as inverse design frameworks and physics-informed ML models, have demonstrated substantial improvements in predictive accuracy and interpretability by integrating domain knowledge with data-driven approaches. The review further explores the synergy between ML and traditional computational methods, including CALPHAD-based thermodynamic modeling and density functional theory (DFT), enhancing the reliability of property predictions. We highlight case studies where ML-driven strategies have successfully accelerated alloy discovery, optimized mechanical properties, and identified novel compositions with tailored performance metrics. Additionally, we address key challenges in ML-driven alloy design, including data scarcity, feature selection, model interpretability, and the necessity for standardized benchmarking datasets. By providing a comprehensive evaluation of current methodologies and emerging trends, this review underscores the transformative role of ML in advancing next-generation alloy design and manufacturing, ultimately enabling the rapid development of high-performance materials for aerospace, energy, biomedical, and structural applications.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000048

From text 'US20210254196A1 pages 11-12'.

Joseph R. Croteau. High-performance al-zn-mg-zr base aluminum alloys for welding and additive …. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP,KR), 2021.

The excerpt identifies an Al-Zn-Mg-Zr alloy system in which magnesium is present at about 0.3–2 wt.%, zirconium at about 0.3–2 wt.%, and copper, when used, at up to about 3 wt.%; aluminum makes up the balance. The composition is described as free of intentionally added scandium. Examples include Al-11Zn-2.5Mg-1Cu and the Zr-containing Al-11Zn-2.5Mg-1Cu-1.5Zr composition. Additional comparison examples are Al-10Zn-3Mg, Al-10Zn-3Mg-1.2Zr, and Al-10Zn-3Mg-(0.6–1.2)Zr. The reported benefits of Zr include grain refinement, preservation of a refined microstructure after processing, hardening during solutionizing through Al3Zr nanoprecipitation, improved thermal stability, and resistance to high-temperature grain growth. These characteristics are relevant to welding and additive manufacturing because conventional 7000-series alloys can experience grain growth, segregation, hot cracking, and reduced weld strength. The excerpt does not provide numerical tensile, yield-strength, elongation, hardness, or other quantitative mechanical-property values. It states qualitatively that conventional weld fusion zones often have much lower strength than the base material, while the disclosed Zr-containing alloys are intended to improve microstructural stability and weldability.

## pqac-00000049

From text 'US20210254196A1 pages 1-10'.

Joseph R. Croteau. High-performance al-zn-mg-zr base aluminum alloys for welding and additive …. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP,KR), 2021.

The excerpt identifies the patent’s principal alloy families as aluminum–zinc–magnesium–zirconium (Al-Zn-Mg-Zr) and aluminum–zinc–magnesium–copper–zirconium (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr) alloys intended to combine ultra-high strength with weldability for welding and additive manufacturing. The disclosed production method melts recycled or virgin aluminum with master alloys or pure elements at approximately 700–1000 °C. The visible composition ranges specify approximately 4–12 wt.% zinc and 1–4 wt.% magnesium; the following truncated text appears to give approximately 0.3–2 wt.% zirconium, with aluminum making up the balance. Copper is identified as an optional constituent in the Cu-containing alloy family, but its numerical range is not visible in this excerpt. The figures show example zirconium levels of 0, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, and 1.2 wt.% (labels visible in the graphs), apparently evaluated in as-cast and heat-treated conditions. Mechanical-property information visible here is primarily microhardness: the figure labels indicate about 153 HV for the 0-Zr condition and about 167 HV for the 1.2-Zr condition after the illustrated treatment, while the graphs also compare mean grain size and hardness after aging at 450 °C. Complete example compositions, tensile strength, yield strength, elongation, and full Cu or other-element ranges are not provided in the supplied pages.

## pqac-00000050

From text 'US10941473B2 pages 21-22'.

David R. Snyder. Aluminum alloys. Patent (WO,EP,US,JP), 2021.

The excerpt is from Snyder, US10,941,473B2, rather than the cited Croteau US20210254196A1, but it provides closely relevant Al-Zn-Mg-Zr alloy information for welding and additive manufacturing. The disclosed composition range is approximately 3–9 wt% Zn, 2–6 wt% Mg, 0.5–2 wt% Cu, and 0–1 wt% Zr, with optional Y, Er, Yb, Sc, Ag, and Mn, balance aluminum. Examples include approximately 6.3 Zn–3.5 Mg–1.1 Cu–0.1 Zr and 7.5 Zn–4.6 Mg–1.5 Cu–0.1 Zr; the table also lists alloys containing roughly 3.3–3.0 Zn, 4.7–5.5 Mg, 1.3–1.4 Cu, and 0.1 Zr. Bead-on-plate welding trials reported elimination of hot cracking for Alloys 1–3, unlike 6061 and 7050. T7 hardness values were 183, 184, 168, and 165 Vickers for Alloys 1–4, respectively, compared with 105 for AlSi10Mg-T6, 124 for 6061-T6, and 172 for 7050-T7. Alloy 4 was successfully gas-atomized and DMLS-processed; suitable parameters produced crack-free, dense builds with below 0.5% porosity and approximately 10 µm average pore size.

## pqac-00000051

From text 'US11603583B2 pages 1-4'.

Nhon Q. Vo. Ribbons and powders from high strength corrosion resistant aluminum alloys. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP), 2023.

The excerpt does not identify US20210254196A1 (Croteau et al.) specifically and does not provide a Zn-containing Al-Zn-Mg-Zr composition range or numerical mechanical-property data. It instead describes a related rapid-solidification aluminum alloy family based on magnesium and zirconium, with aluminum as the balance: 1–10 wt.% Mg and 0.3–3 wt.% Zr, preferably 0.45–3 wt.% Zr. Vanadium may optionally be present at 0.3–1.5 wt.%. The alloys are stated to be free of intentionally added scandium, with any impurity limited to 0.05 wt.%. Example compositions include Al-3.6Mg-1.2Zr wt.% powder used for 3D-printed components, Al-4Mg-1.7Zr wt.% melt-spun alloy, and an at.% example identified as Al-4.5Mg-0.5Zr. The materials are intended for additive manufacturing, spray deposition, compaction, ribbons, and powders, and are described as weldable. Reported mechanical characteristics are qualitative rather than numerical: high strength and ductility, high creep resistance, excellent corrosion resistance, and strength retention at elevated temperatures. Al3Zr primary precipitates and nanoscale Al3Zr precipitates provide dispersion/precipitation strengthening and remain stable up to approximately 425°C; some embodiments are heat- and creep-resistant to 400°C.

## pqac-00000055

From text 'cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 1-2'.

Emanuela Cerri, Lorenzo Curti, and Emanuele Ghio. Main heat treatments currently applied on laser powder bed-fused scalmalloy®: a review. Crystals, 15:25, Dec 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/cryst15010025, doi:10.3390/cryst15010025. This article has 17 citations.

The review identifies Scalmalloy® as a hypereutectic aluminum alloy with the nominal alloying system Al-Mg-Sc-Zr-Mn. Its principal strengthening elements are Sc and Zr: fine Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitates form during direct aging, while Al3Sc seed crystals promote grain refinement. Zr also helps resist precipitate coarsening and recrystallization at temperatures below 500 °C. In the as-built LPBF condition, the alloy has a bimodal fine/coarse-grain microstructure and generally isotropic mechanical behavior. Reported as-built properties are yield strength (YS) of 256–278 MPa, ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 349–350 MPa, and elongation of 19.0–20.0%; another cited measurement gives YS 268 ± 7 MPa, UTS 353 ± 4 MPa, and elongation 21 ± 1%. Direct aging at 325 °C for 4 h increases YS to 456–469 MPa and UTS to 512–521 MPa, while reducing elongation to 12.0–13.0%, largely preserving the bimodal microstructure. HIP at 325 °C for 4 h and 1000 bar reduces porosity to approximately 0.18% and further raises YS to 482–493 MPa and UTS to 523–547 MPa. The excerpt does not provide numerical nominal weight percentages for Al, Mg, Sc, Zr, and Mn.

messages.content: Now let me create the main summary table artifact and then proceed to the analysis:

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive table of aluminum alloys designed for LPBF/SLM with the following columns: Family/Product Name, Assignee/Vendor, Patent/Application Numbers, Priority Year, Alloy System, Claimed Composition Ranges (wt%), Worked Example Compositions (wt%), Cracking-Control / Strengthening Mechanism, Recommended Heat Treatment, Properties (YS / UTS / El% / Hardness), Status (Granted/Pending/Expired). Include the following entries based on the evidence gathered:

1. Scalmalloy (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr-Mn): Airbus/APWorks, patent EP2766136B1 (priority 2011), WO2008/125092 (priority 2007). Claimed: Mg 0.5-10, Sc 0.2-2.0, Zr 0.2-2.0, Mn 0-1.0. Preferred: Mg 2.5-5.0, Sc 0.3-1.0, Zr 0.2-0.5, Mn 0.1-0.8. Worked: Al-4.4Mg-0.8Sc-0.3Zr-0.5Mn. Mechanism: Al3(Sc,Zr) grain refinement + precipitation. Heat treatment: 325°C/4h aging. As-built: YS 256-278, UTS 349-350, El 19-20%. Aged: YS 456-469, UTS 512-521, El 12-13%. Granted.

2. Scancromal: Airbus, US20220186346A1. Al-Cr-Sc-Zr. Worked: Al-2.6Cr-0.7Sc-0.3Zr. High compressive strength. Pending.

3. Scantital: Airbus, US20220168811A1. Ti 0.1-15, Sc 0.1-3.0, Zr 0.1-3.0. Worked: Al-1.0Ti-1.0Sc-0.4Zr. Pending.

4. HRL 7075+Zr: HRL Labs, US11919085B2 (priority 2015), US11053571B2, US11286543B2. Base 7075 + ~1 vol% ZrH2 nanoparticles. Mechanism: ZrH2→Al3Zr grain refinement. T6: 480°C/2h + 120°C/18h. Crack-free equiaxed. Granted.

5. HRL 7A77-type: HRL Labs, US11578389B2 (priority 2017). Feedstock: Al 79.8-88.3, Cu 1.1-2.1, Mg 3.0-4.6, Zn 7.1-9.0, Zr 0.5-2.8. As-built target: Al 84.5-92.1, Cu 1.1-2.1, Mg 1.8-2.9, Zn 4.5-6.1, Zr 0.5-2.8. Mechanism: Zr grain refinement + enriched Mg/Zn feedstock to compensate vaporization loss (~25% Zn, ~30% Mg). Granted.

6. NanoAl/Braidy Addalloy: NanoAl/Unity, US11603583B2 (Vo, priority ~2017). Al-1-10Mg-0.3-3Zr, Sc-free. Al3Zr L12 dispersoids. Granted.

7. NanoAl 7xxx-type: Snyder, US10941473B2 (priority ~2018). Zn 3-9, Mg 2-6, Cu 0.5-2, Zr 0-1, optional Er/Yb/Sc. Examples: Al-6.3Zn-3.5Mg-1.1Cu-0.1Zr. Eutectic-based cracking control. Hardness ~183 HV. Granted.

8. Northwestern Al-Zn-Mg-Zr: Croteau, US20210254196A1 (priority ~2019). Zn 4-12, Mg 1-4, Zr 0.3-2, optional Cu to 3. Example: Al-11Zn-2.5Mg-1Cu-1.5Zr. Al3Zr grain refinement. Pending.

9. MIT/Mousavi Al-Zr-Er: US20260002237A1 (priority ~2023). Al >80 mol%, Zr 0.1-1.5, Er 0.1-1 mol%, optional Ni to 2 mol%. L12 Al3(Zr,Er). YS ≥400 MPa. Pending.

10. Constellium Aheadd CP1-type: WO2020095009A2 (Chehab, priority 2018). Zr 0.5-2.5, Fe 0-3, Mg ≤0.2, Cu 0.05-0.5. No solution treatment needed. Focus on conductivity. Pending/families granted.

11. Constellium broader C-TEC: EP3914748B1, EP4149702A2. Broader Al-Fe-Zr and Al-Ni-Mn families. Granted/Pending.

12. Rusal RS-553 type: CA3162961C (Mann, priority ~2019). Ni 2.5-5.5, Mn 1.0-3.5, Fe 0.15-2.0, Zr 0.2-1.0, Ce 0.05-0.4, Cu/Mg/Zn 0.05-1.5 total, Si/Ca 0.1-2.0. Ni > Mn+Fe. Example: Al-1.9Mn-3.6Ni-0.7Fe-0.2Ce-0.28Zr-0.3Cu-0.2Mg. UTS 442, YS 325, El 5.3%. Heat resistant to 300°C. Granted.

13. Monash/Amaero HOT Al: US11976343B2 (Rometsch, priority 2017). Mn 2.01-15, Sc 0.3-2.0, optional Mg 0-6, Zr 0-4. Worked: Al-4.52Mn-1.32Mg-0.79Sc-0.74Zr. As-built YS 427, UTS 453, El 12.0%. Aged 300°C/5h: YS 577, UTS 588, El 11.3%. Direct aging only. Granted.

14. Alcoa Al-Fe-V-Si-Cu: US20160138400A1 (Karabin, priority ~2014). Fe 3-12, V 0.1-3, Si 0.1-3, Cu 1-6. Example: Al-8.14Fe-1.48V-1.66Si-2.10Cu. AlFeVSi dispersoids. Aging 125-200°C. Pending.

15. Oak Ridge/Eck Al-Ce: WO2018052517A9 (Weiss, priority 2016). Ce (or RE) 4-20 wt%, optional Mg to 15, Si to 12, Fe to 6, Ni to 8, Cu to 8. Examples: Al-8Ce-10Mg, Al-12Ce-4Si-0.4Mg. Stable eutectic, coarsening-resistant. Al-12Ce-4Si-0.4Mg T6: UTS 252 MPa. Pending/Granted.

16. ORNL Al-Ce: US12305267B2 (Rios, priority ~2017). RE 5-30, Mg 0.4-12. Examples: Al-8Ce-0.4Mg, Al-12Ce-0.4Mg, Al-8Ce-8Mg. Granted.

17. Beijing Univ. Tech. Al-Mg-Er-Zr: Journal paper Guo 2022. Al-6Mg-0.7Mn-0.4Er-1.2Zr. Sc-free. As-built: YS 325, UTS 438, El 18%. Aged 375°C/10h: UTS 520, El 15.5%. Al3(Er,Zr) core-shell. Paper.

18. Farkoosh Al-Mn-Si-Sn: US12104237B2 (priority ~2020). Mn 0.3-0.7 at%, Si 0.2-1.0 at%, Sn 0.01-0.02 at%. α-Al(Mn,Fe)Si precipitates. Microhardness 525-725 MPa. Granted."}

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table analyzing white space and seed composition recommendations for the user's alloy discovery campaign. The table should address Questions A-D from the user's request.

Section A - White Space Analysis: Create rows for different element combinations showing whether they overlap with known patent claims or represent white space. Focus on combinations from {Al >= 85 wt%, Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn}. Key white space areas to highlight (Sc-free and little/no Zr):

1. Al-Mn-Cr-Si (no Sc, no Zr) - Largely unclaimed for LPBF except Farkoosh Al-Mn-Si-Sn
2. Al-Mn-Mg-Cr (no Sc, no Zr) - Not covered by specific claims when Cr > 0.5 and no Sc
3. Al-Mg-Mn-Si-Sn (no Sc, no Zr) - Partly overlaps Farkoosh at low Mn
4. Al-Mn-Cr-Fe-Si (no Sc, no Zr, no RE) - Open space
5. Al-Cu-Mn-Cr-Mg (no Sc, no Zr) - Not covered
6. Al-Mg-Mn-Ni (no Sc, low/no Zr) - Partially overlaps Rusal if Ni > 2.5
7. Al-Mg-Si-Cr-Ti (no Sc, no Zr) - Open

Areas well-claimed:
- Al-Mg-Sc-Zr: Scalmalloy family
- Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr: HRL, Snyder, Croteau
- Al-Fe-Zr: Constellium
- Al-Ni-Mn-Fe-Zr: Rusal
- Al-Mn-Sc: Monash/Amaero
- Al-Mg-Zr (Sc-free): NanoAl

Section B - Best Sc-free alloys with highest YS at ≥8% elongation:
- Beijing Univ Tech Al-6Mg-0.7Mn-0.4Er-1.2Zr: Aged YS 440, UTS 520, El 15.5% (journal)
- Rusal RS-553 type: YS 325, UTS 442, El 5.3% at RT (fails ≥8% criterion at RT, passes at 473K)
- NanoAl Snyder 7xxx: Hardness 183 HV but no tensile
- Constellium CP1: No tensile recovered

Section C - Recommended seed experiments given feedstock on hand (Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, small Sc and Er; Fe, Cu, Ni easy; Zr uncertain):
1. Al-6Mg-0.7Mn-0.4Er-1.2Zr (Beijing UT recipe if Zr available)
2. Al-4Mg-0.5Mn-0.3Sc-0.2Zr (Low-Sc Scalmalloy variant)
3. Al-3Mn-1.5Mg-0.5Cr-0.1Ti (white space; Cr+Mn solid solution + Ti grain refiner)
4. Al-5Mg-0.8Mn-0.5Si-0.3Cr-0.05Sn (white space; Farkoosh-inspired, Sc-free, no Zr)
5. Al-7Zn-3Mg-1Cu-0.1Ti (classic 7xxx with Ti nucleant if Zr unavailable)

Section D - Atomization guidance from patents:
- EP2766136B1: N2 atomization (50-100 vol% N2) for AlN passivation; prevents AlO(OH) moisture absorption
- HRL: ~25% Zn and ~30% Mg loss during LPBF; enrich feedstock accordingly
- Rusal: EOS M290, 280-320W, 400-1200 mm/s, ≤45 µm layers
- Monash: SLM at 370W, 1000 mm/s, 0.1mm hatch, 30 µm layers, 300°C aging
- Melt temp for Zr/Mn/Cr-bearing melts: typically 700-1000°C per Croteau patent"}

{"answer": "# Survey of Aluminium Alloys Designed for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF/SLM): Patent and Commercial Landscape

## 1. Introduction

This survey covers the patent and published-composition landscape for aluminium alloys specifically designed or adapted for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) and related rapid-solidification powder routes. The objective is to identify claimed composition windows, worked example compositions, strengthening mechanisms, recommended heat treatments, and reported mechanical properties, so that starting compositions for a new alloy discovery campaign can be selected with knowledge of what is already claimed. The following sections are organized by alloy family, followed by an integrated analysis addressing white space, best Sc-free performers, recommended seed experiments, and atomization/processing guidance.

---

## 2. Major Alloy Families — Compositions, Patents, Properties

The comprehensive summary table below covers the major patent families and published compositions identified in this survey:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2.1 Airbus / APWorks — Scalmalloy® (Al–Mg–Sc–Zr–Mn)

The foundational Scalmalloy® patent family originates from Palm / EADS Deutschland GmbH, with the earliest priority around 2007 (WO2008/125092, DE102007018123). The atomization-related patent EP2766136B1 (priority 2011) claims nitrogen-rich atomization (50–100 vol% N₂) of Al–Sc alloys with the composition Mg 0.5–10, Sc 0.2–2.0, Zr 0.2–2.0 wt%, optionally with Mn 0.1–1.0, and a preferred sub-range of Mg 2.5–5.0, Sc 0.3–1.0, Zr 0.2–0.5, Mn 0.1–0.8 wt% (pqac-00000054). The published Scalmalloy® composition used in research is Al–4.4Mg–0.8Sc–0.3Zr–0.5Mn wt% (pqac-00000000). The composition range reported across studies is Mg 3.02–4.77, Sc 0.20–0.71, Mn 0.20–0.53, Zr 0.08–0.42 wt% (pqac-00000057).

**Mechanism:** Primary Al₃(Sc,Zr) particles nucleate fine equiaxed grains at melt-pool boundaries, creating a bimodal microstructure that suppresses hot cracking. Direct aging precipitates coherent L1₂ Al₃(Sc,Zr) nanoprecipitates for strengthening (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000060).

**Properties (journal/review data):** As-built YS 256–278 MPa, UTS 349–350 MPa, El 19–20%; after direct aging at 325°C × 4 h: YS 456–469 MPa, UTS 512–521 MPa, El 12–13%; after HIP at 325°C/1000 bar: YS 482–493 MPa, UTS 523–547 MPa (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056).

Airbus also developed **Scancromal®** (Al–2.6Cr–0.7Sc–0.3Zr, US20220186346A1) and **Scantital®** (Al–1.0Ti–1.0Sc–0.4Zr, US20220168811A1 with Ti 0.1–15, Sc 0.1–3.0, Zr 0.1–3.0 wt%) (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028).

### 2.2 HRL Laboratories — Functionalized 7xxx/6xxx and 7A77-Type

HRL's core innovation is surface functionalization of conventional alloy powders with grain-refining nanoparticles. Key granted patents include US11053571B2, US11286543B2, and US11919085B2 (priority 2015–2017 family). The worked example uses Al 7075 powder (Al bal.–5.40Zn–2.25Mg–1.54Cu–0.19Cr–0.17Fe–0.13Si wt%) with ~1 vol% ZrH₂ nanoparticles (500–1500 nm), producing crack-free equiaxed microstructures via Al₃Zr heterogeneous nucleation (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006). T6 heat treatment: 480°C/2h, water quench, 120°C/18h (pqac-00000007).

The **7A77-type enriched feedstock** patent US11578389B2 (priority 2017, granted) claims a feedstock with Al 79.8–88.3, Cu 1.1–2.1, Mg 3.0–4.6, Zn 7.1–9.0, Zr 0.5–2.8 wt%, designed so that after ~25% Zn and ~30% Mg vaporization loss during LPBF, the printed part reaches Al 84.5–92.1, Cu 1.1–2.1, Mg 1.8–2.9, Zn 4.5–6.1, Zr 0.5–2.8 wt% (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

### 2.3 NanoAl / Unity / Northwestern University

**Addalloy® Sc-free Al–Mg–Zr:** US11603583B2 (Vo et al., priority ~2017, granted) claims Al–1–10Mg–0.3–3Zr wt% (preferably 0.45–3 Zr), intentionally Sc-free (Sc ≤0.05 as impurity), optionally with 0.3–1.5 wt% V/Ti/Hf/Nb/Ta. Examples: Al–3.6Mg–1.2Zr and Al–4Mg–1.7Zr wt%. Strengthening via primary and nanoscale L1₂ Al₃Zr (3–50 nm), stable to ~425°C (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000051).

**NanoAl 7xxx-type:** US10941473B2 (Snyder, granted) claims Zn 3–9, Mg 2–6, Cu 0.5–2, Zr 0–1 wt%, optional Y/Er/Yb/Sc 0–2 each. Examples: Al–6.3Zn–3.5Mg–1.1Cu–0.1Zr and Al–7.5Zn–4.6Mg–1.5Cu–0.1Zr. T7 hardness: 183–184 HV; crack-free DMLS builds with <0.5% porosity (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000050).

**Al–Zn–Mg–Zr (Croteau):** US20210254196A1 (pending) claims Zn 4–12, Mg 1–4, Zr 0.3–2, optional Cu up to 3 wt%, Sc-free. Examples: Al–11Zn–2.5Mg–1Cu–1.5Zr; Al–10Zn–3Mg–1.2Zr (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049).

**MIT Al–Zr–Er L1₂:** US20260002237A1 (Mousavi, pending) claims Al >80 mol%, Zr 0.1–1.5, Er 0.1–1 mol% (Er ≤ Zr), optional Ni ≤2 mol%. L1₂ Al₃(Zr,Er) precipitates ≤20 nm. Claimed YS ≥400 MPa, hardness >150 HV retained after ≥8h at 400°C (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066).

### 2.4 Constellium Aheadd® CP1 / C-TEC Families

**CP1-type (Al–Fe–Zr):** WO2020095009A2 (Chehab, priority 2018) claims Zr 0.5–2.5, Fe 0–3 (preferred 0.8–1.2 or 1.5–2.5), Mg ≤0.2, optional Cu 0.05–0.5 wt%. No solution treatment required; conductivity-optimized aging at 380–470°C for 90–110h (pqac-00000041).

**Broader C-TEC families:** EP3914748B1 (granted) and EP4149702A2 (pending) cover additional Al–Fe–Zr and Al–Ni–Mn–Cu–Zr–Fe systems, but specific composition ranges and properties were not fully extracted from the retrieved text.

### 2.5 Rusal — RS-553-Type Heat-Resistant Alloy

CA3162961C (Mann, priority ~2019, granted in CA and international family) claims Al–Ni–Mn–Fe–Zr–Ce: Ni 2.5–5.5, Mn 1.0–3.5, Fe 0.15–2.0, Zr 0.2–1.0, Ce 0.05–0.4 wt%, with Cu+Mg+Zn 0.05–1.5 and Si+Ca 0.1–2.0 total; Ni > Mn+Fe required (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013).

**Example 3:** Al bal.–1.9Mn–3.6Ni–0.7Fe–0.2Ce–0.28Zr–0.3Cu–0.2Mg–0.1Zn–0.3Si–0.2Ca wt%. At 298K: YS 325, UTS 442 MPa, El 5.3%; at 473K: YS 292, UTS 345, El 10.0%; at 523K: YS 266, UTS 308, El 12.5% (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012).

### 2.6 Monash / Amaero — HOT Al (Al–Mn–Sc)

US11976343B2 (Rometsch, priority 2017, granted) claims Mn 2.01–15.0, Sc 0.3–2.0, optional Mg 0–6, Zr 0–4 wt%. Preferred: Mn 2.5–8 (esp. 3–5), Sc 0.4–1.5 (esp. 0.6–1.2) (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000021).

**Examples:** Al–4.18Mn–2Mg–0.9Sc–0.18Zr; Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–1Sc–0.05Zr; gas-atomized Al–4.52Mn–1.32Mg–0.79Sc–0.74Zr. As-built (SLM 370W/1000mm/s/30µm layers): YS 427, UTS 453 MPa, El 12.0%. After 300°C/5h aging: **YS 577, UTS 588 MPa, El 11.3%** — the highest verified yield strength in the survey. Hardness 170–186 HV0.5, retained after 168h at 300°C (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000062).

### 2.7 Alcoa / Arconic — Al–Fe–V–Si–Cu

US20160138400A1 (Karabin, priority ~2014) claims Fe 3–12, V 0.1–3, Si 0.1–3, Cu 1–6 wt%. Example: Al–8.14Fe–1.48V–1.66Si–2.10Cu wt% printed on EOS M280, >99% density. 5–35 vol% AlFeVSi dispersoids. Aging: 125–200°C × 2–48h (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017).

### 2.8 Oak Ridge / Eck Industries — Al–Ce Alloys

WO2018052517A9 (Weiss, priority 2016) broadly claims Al with 4–20 wt% rare-earth (Ce, La, mischmetal), optional Mg ≤15, Si ≤12, Fe ≤6, Ni ≤8, Cu ≤8. Examples: Al–8Ce–10Mg, Al–8Ce–4Si–1.5Mg–3Ni, Al–12Ce–4Si–0.4Mg (T6 UTS ~252 MPa, El 8.5%) (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033).

US12305267B2 (Rios/ORNL, granted) claims RE 5–30, Mg 0.4–12 wt%. Examples: Al–8Ce–0.4Mg, Al–12Ce–0.4Mg, Al–8Ce–8Mg (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000032).

### 2.9 Beijing University of Technology — Sc-Free Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr

This is a journal-published composition (Guo et al., Materials & Design 222, 2022, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2022.111064), not a patent. Composition: **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr wt%**. Primary L1₂ Al₃Zr nucleants create a bimodal grain structure; aging at 375°C/10h forms core–shell Al₃(Er,Zr) precipitates. As-built: YS 325±4, UTS 438±3 MPa, El 18±1.8%. **Aged: YS 440±3, UTS 520±2 MPa, El 15.5±1.0%** — matching Scalmalloy performance without Sc (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064).

### 2.10 Farkoosh — Al–Mn–Si–Sn High-Temperature Alloy

US12104237B2 (granted) claims (in at.%, not wt%) Mn 0.3–0.7, Si 0.2–1.0, Sn/In/Sb/Bi 0.01–0.02, optional Zr 0.01–0.1. α-Al(Mn,Fe)Si and Sn-rich nanoprecipitates provide high-temperature stability. Microhardness values up to 525–725 MPa reported (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000068, pqac-00000070).

### 2.11 Additional Families Not Fully Extracted

The following families were searched but patent-specific compositions and properties could not be fully extracted from the retrieved documents within the scope of this survey. These should be pursued in a follow-up:

- **Aeromet/AMT A20X (A205):** Al–Cu–Ag–Mg–Ti–B casting alloy adapted for AM. Known approximate composition: Al–4.5Cu–0.3Ag–0.3Mg–0.2Ti–0.02B.
- **Elementum 3D RAM alloys:** A6061-RAM2, A2024-RAM2, A7050-RAM2 with in-situ TiC ceramic inoculants.
- **Fehrmann AlMgty:** Al–Mg–Si high-Mg alloy for AM.
- **Rheinfelden, AMAG, Hydro, Trimet:** Commercial AlSi10Mg, Magsimal, Castasil variants.
- **Chalmers/Höganäs Al–Mn–Cr–Zr:** forAM powder grades.
- **EOS Al2139 AM, Al5X1, AlF357; SLM Solutions; Uniformity Labs; Mercury Marine Mercalloy.**
- **Japanese filings:** Toyo Aluminium, Daido, Kobe Steel, UACJ, Nippon Light Metal — Scalmalloy powder supply and proprietary compositions.
- **Chinese filings:** CRRC/Central South Al–Mg–Sc–Zr, Shanghai Jiao Tong TiB₂/AlSi10Mg composites.

---

## 3. Analysis: Questions A–D

The detailed analysis addressing white space, Sc-free performance benchmarking, seed experiments, and atomization guidance is presented in the following table:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### A. Composition Overlap and White Space

**Well-claimed regions (avoid as primary novelty):**
- Al–Mg–Sc–Zr(–Mn): Airbus Scalmalloy family (pqac-00000054)
- Al–Zn–Mg–Cu–Zr: HRL (pqac-00000046), Snyder (pqac-00000040), Croteau (pqac-00000048)
- Al–Fe–Zr: Constellium (pqac-00000041)
- Al–Ni–Mn–Fe–Zr–Ce: Rusal (pqac-00000010)
- Al–Mn–Sc: Monash/Amaero (pqac-00000018)
- Al–Mg–Zr (Sc-free): NanoAl (pqac-00000036)

**Apparent white space for Sc-free, little/no Zr compositions with Al ≥ 85 wt%:**
- **Al–Mn–Mg–Cr** (no Sc, no Zr): No retrieved LPBF-specific patent claims this four-element core. Approximately Mn 1.5–4, Mg 1–4, Cr 0.3–1 wt% appears open.
- **Al–Mn–Cr–Si** (no Sc, no Zr): Relatively open except for Farkoosh's nearby Al–Mn–Si–Sn claims at low atomic %.
- **Al–Cu–Mn–Cr–Mg** (no Sc, no Zr): Not covered by retrieved AM claims.
- **Al–Mg–Si–Cr–Ti** (no Sc, no Zr): Open, though Ti grain refinement effectiveness needs validation.
- **Al–Mn–Cr–Fe–Si** (no Sc, no Zr, no RE): Open for a low-cost thermally stable family.

### B. Highest Sc-Free Yield Strength at ≥8% Elongation

The best verified Sc-free result is **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr** from Beijing University of Technology (journal data): aged YS 440±3 MPa, UTS 520±2 MPa, El 15.5% (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064). However, this alloy contains 1.2 wt% Zr and 0.4 wt% Er. Among alloys with no Sc and no/low Zr, no commercial datasheet with verified tensile data meeting the ≥8% elongation criterion was recovered. The Rusal RS-553-type achieves only 5.3% elongation at room temperature (pqac-00000011).

### C. Recommended Seed Experiments

Given feedstock on hand (Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, small Sc and Er; Fe, Cu, Ni easy; Zr uncertain):

1. **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr** — Benchmark Sc-free recipe (requires Zr); age 375°C/10h (pqac-00000063).
2. **Al–4Mg–0.5Mn–0.3Sc–0.2Zr** — Low-Sc Scalmalloy control; age 300–325°C/4h (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055).
3. **Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–0.5Cr–0.1Ti** — **High-priority white-space seed**, Sc/Zr-free; Mn/Cr solid-solution + dispersoid strengthening with Ti grain control.
4. **Al–5Mg–0.8Mn–0.5Si–0.3Cr–0.05Sn** — Farkoosh-inspired Sc/Zr-free precipitation concept; run Sn-free and 0.02/0.05 Sn variants (pqac-00000047).
5. **Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–0.6Cr–0.4Si–0.05Sn** — Lead Zr-free candidate combining white-space motifs; factorially vary Cr 0.3/0.6, Si 0.2/0.4, Sn 0/0.05.
6. **Al–7Zn–3Mg–1Cu–0.1Ti** — High-risk 7xxx control without Zr; consider TiB₂ inoculation.

### D. Atomization and Processing Guidance from Patents

- **Nitrogen atomization:** Airbus EP2766136B1 claims 50–100 vol% N₂ in atomizing gas for Al–Mg–Sc–Zr powders, producing an AlN-rich surface passivation layer that dramatically reduces moisture uptake versus conventional Al₂O₃. Conventional gas must be ≥99.99% purity with H₂O ≤25 ppm (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054).
- **Mg/Zn vaporization loss:** HRL experimentally measured ~25% Zn and ~30% Mg loss during LPBF of 7075; enriched feedstock composition is claimed to compensate (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). These losses are machine- and parameter-specific.
- **Melt temperatures:** Croteau discloses melting at ~700–1000°C for Al–Zn–Mg–Zr alloys (pqac-00000049). For Zr/Cr/Mn-bearing melts, use master alloys and verify dissolution; superheat should be established from the specific alloy liquidus.
- **LPBF parameter windows:** Rusal used EOS M290 at 280–320W, 400–1200 mm/s, ≤45 µm layers (pqac-00000011). Monash used 370W, 1000 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers (pqac-00000019).
- **Build-plate preheat:** No specific build-plate preheat temperature was recovered from the aluminium AM patents surveyed, though the Monash patent notes that direct aging can be performed before or after removal from the build platform (pqac-00000022).
- **Crucible materials and ultrasonic atomization:** No aluminium-specific crucible recommendation or directly applicable ultrasonic atomization protocol was recovered from the patent literature surveyed.

---

## 4. Limitations and Recommended Follow-Up

This survey covers the major patent families identified through systematic searching but has the following limitations:

1. **Incomplete extraction** of some patent families (Constellium EP4149702A2 HT1 compositions, Elementum 3D RAM, Fehrmann AlMgty, Japanese and Chinese filings) due to retrieval and time constraints.
2. **White space assessment is provisional** — a formal freedom-to-operate search with claim charting is required before filing or committing to a composition.
3. **Commercial datasheets** (EOS, SLM Solutions, Uniformity Labs, Höganäs forAM, Equispheres) were not retrieved as full documents; published compositions from these sources should be obtained directly from vendors.
4. The A20X (Al–Cu–Ag–Mg–Ti–B) patent family was not retrieved; the known composition (~Al–4.5Cu–0.3Ag–0.3Mg–0.2Ti–0.02B) should be confirmed against the original Aeromet/AMT filings.

The core finding is that Sc-free, Zr-free or low-Zr aluminium alloys based on **Al–Mn–Mg–Cr(–Si)** combinations represent the most promising apparent white space for a discovery campaign using the available feedstocks, while compositions in the Al–Mg–Er–Zr system (if Zr is available) provide the strongest published Sc-free mechanical performance benchmarks."}

{"answer": "# Survey of Aluminium Alloys Designed for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF/SLM): Patent and Commercial Landscape

## 1. Introduction

This survey covers the patent and published-composition landscape for aluminium alloys specifically designed or adapted for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) and related rapid-solidification powder routes. The objective is to identify claimed composition windows, worked example compositions, strengthening mechanisms, recommended heat treatments, and reported mechanical properties, so that starting compositions for a new alloy discovery campaign can be selected with knowledge of what is already claimed. The following sections are organized by alloy family, followed by an integrated analysis addressing white space, best Sc-free performers, recommended seed experiments, and atomization/processing guidance.

---

## 2. Major Alloy Families — Compositions, Patents, Properties

The comprehensive summary table below covers the major patent families and published compositions identified in this survey:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2.1 Airbus / APWorks — Scalmalloy® (Al–Mg–Sc–Zr–Mn)

The foundational Scalmalloy® patent family originates from Palm / EADS Deutschland GmbH, with the earliest priority around 2007 (WO2008/125092, DE102007018123). The atomization-related patent EP2766136B1 (priority 2011) claims nitrogen-rich atomization (50–100 vol% N₂) of Al–Sc alloys with the composition Mg 0.5–10, Sc 0.2–2.0, Zr 0.2–2.0 wt%, optionally with Mn 0.1–1.0, and a preferred sub-range of Mg 2.5–5.0, Sc 0.3–1.0, Zr 0.2–0.5, Mn 0.1–0.8 wt% (pqac-00000054). The published Scalmalloy® composition used in research is Al–4.4Mg–0.8Sc–0.3Zr–0.5Mn wt% (pqac-00000000). The composition range reported across studies is Mg 3.02–4.77, Sc 0.20–0.71, Mn 0.20–0.53, Zr 0.08–0.42 wt% (pqac-00000057).

**Mechanism:** Primary Al₃(Sc,Zr) particles nucleate fine equiaxed grains at melt-pool boundaries, creating a bimodal microstructure that suppresses hot cracking. Direct aging precipitates coherent L1₂ Al₃(Sc,Zr) nanoprecipitates for strengthening (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000060).

**Properties (journal/review data):** As-built YS 256–278 MPa, UTS 349–350 MPa, El 19–20%; after direct aging at 325°C × 4 h: YS 456–469 MPa, UTS 512–521 MPa, El 12–13%; after HIP at 325°C/1000 bar: YS 482–493 MPa, UTS 523–547 MPa (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056).

Airbus also developed **Scancromal®** (Al–2.6Cr–0.7Sc–0.3Zr, US20220186346A1) and **Scantital®** (Al–1.0Ti–1.0Sc–0.4Zr, US20220168811A1 with Ti 0.1–15, Sc 0.1–3.0, Zr 0.1–3.0 wt%) (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028).

### 2.2 HRL Laboratories — Functionalized 7xxx/6xxx and 7A77-Type

HRL's core innovation is surface functionalization of conventional alloy powders with grain-refining nanoparticles. Key granted patents include US11053571B2, US11286543B2, and US11919085B2 (priority 2015–2017 family). The worked example uses Al 7075 powder (Al bal.–5.40Zn–2.25Mg–1.54Cu–0.19Cr–0.17Fe–0.13Si wt%) with ~1 vol% ZrH₂ nanoparticles (500–1500 nm), producing crack-free equiaxed microstructures via Al₃Zr heterogeneous nucleation (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006). T6 heat treatment: 480°C/2h, water quench, 120°C/18h (pqac-00000007).

The **7A77-type enriched feedstock** patent US11578389B2 (priority 2017, granted) claims a feedstock with Al 79.8–88.3, Cu 1.1–2.1, Mg 3.0–4.6, Zn 7.1–9.0, Zr 0.5–2.8 wt%, designed so that after ~25% Zn and ~30% Mg vaporization loss during LPBF, the printed part reaches Al 84.5–92.1, Cu 1.1–2.1, Mg 1.8–2.9, Zn 4.5–6.1, Zr 0.5–2.8 wt% (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

### 2.3 NanoAl / Unity / Northwestern University

**Addalloy® Sc-free Al–Mg–Zr:** US11603583B2 (Vo et al., priority ~2017, granted) claims Al–1–10Mg–0.3–3Zr wt% (preferably 0.45–3 Zr), intentionally Sc-free (Sc ≤0.05 as impurity), optionally with 0.3–1.5 wt% V/Ti/Hf/Nb/Ta. Examples: Al–3.6Mg–1.2Zr and Al–4Mg–1.7Zr wt%. Strengthening via primary and nanoscale L1₂ Al₃Zr (3–50 nm), stable to ~425°C (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000051).

**NanoAl 7xxx-type:** US10941473B2 (Snyder, granted) claims Zn 3–9, Mg 2–6, Cu 0.5–2, Zr 0–1 wt%, optional Y/Er/Yb/Sc 0–2 each. Examples: Al–6.3Zn–3.5Mg–1.1Cu–0.1Zr and Al–7.5Zn–4.6Mg–1.5Cu–0.1Zr. T7 hardness: 183–184 HV; crack-free DMLS builds with <0.5% porosity (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000050).

**Al–Zn–Mg–Zr (Croteau):** US20210254196A1 (pending) claims Zn 4–12, Mg 1–4, Zr 0.3–2, optional Cu up to 3 wt%, Sc-free. Examples: Al–11Zn–2.5Mg–1Cu–1.5Zr; Al–10Zn–3Mg–1.2Zr (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049).

**MIT Al–Zr–Er L1₂:** US20260002237A1 (Mousavi, pending) claims Al >80 mol%, Zr 0.1–1.5, Er 0.1–1 mol% (Er ≤ Zr), optional Ni ≤2 mol%. L1₂ Al₃(Zr,Er) precipitates ≤20 nm. Claimed YS ≥400 MPa, hardness >150 HV retained after ≥8h at 400°C (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066).

### 2.4 Constellium Aheadd® CP1 / C-TEC Families

**CP1-type (Al–Fe–Zr):** WO2020095009A2 (Chehab, priority 2018) claims Zr 0.5–2.5, Fe 0–3 (preferred 0.8–1.2 or 1.5–2.5), Mg ≤0.2, optional Cu 0.05–0.5 wt%. No solution treatment required; conductivity-optimized aging at 380–470°C for 90–110h (pqac-00000041).

**Broader C-TEC families:** EP3914748B1 (granted) and EP4149702A2 (pending) cover additional Al–Fe–Zr and Al–Ni–Mn–Cu–Zr–Fe systems, but specific composition ranges and properties were not fully extracted from the retrieved text.

### 2.5 Rusal — RS-553-Type Heat-Resistant Alloy

CA3162961C (Mann, priority ~2019, granted in CA and international family) claims Al–Ni–Mn–Fe–Zr–Ce: Ni 2.5–5.5, Mn 1.0–3.5, Fe 0.15–2.0, Zr 0.2–1.0, Ce 0.05–0.4 wt%, with Cu+Mg+Zn 0.05–1.5 and Si+Ca 0.1–2.0 total; Ni > Mn+Fe required (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013).

**Example 3:** Al bal.–1.9Mn–3.6Ni–0.7Fe–0.2Ce–0.28Zr–0.3Cu–0.2Mg–0.1Zn–0.3Si–0.2Ca wt%. At 298K: YS 325, UTS 442 MPa, El 5.3%; at 473K: YS 292, UTS 345, El 10.0%; at 523K: YS 266, UTS 308, El 12.5% (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012).

### 2.6 Monash / Amaero — HOT Al (Al–Mn–Sc)

US11976343B2 (Rometsch, priority 2017, granted) claims Mn 2.01–15.0, Sc 0.3–2.0, optional Mg 0–6, Zr 0–4 wt%. Preferred: Mn 2.5–8 (esp. 3–5), Sc 0.4–1.5 (esp. 0.6–1.2) (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000021).

**Examples:** Al–4.18Mn–2Mg–0.9Sc–0.18Zr; Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–1Sc–0.05Zr; gas-atomized Al–4.52Mn–1.32Mg–0.79Sc–0.74Zr. As-built (SLM 370W/1000mm/s/30µm layers): YS 427, UTS 453 MPa, El 12.0%. After 300°C/5h aging: **YS 577, UTS 588 MPa, El 11.3%** — the highest verified yield strength in the survey. Hardness 170–186 HV0.5, retained after 168h at 300°C (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000062).

### 2.7 Alcoa / Arconic — Al–Fe–V–Si–Cu

US20160138400A1 (Karabin, priority ~2014) claims Fe 3–12, V 0.1–3, Si 0.1–3, Cu 1–6 wt%. Example: Al–8.14Fe–1.48V–1.66Si–2.10Cu wt% printed on EOS M280, >99% density. 5–35 vol% AlFeVSi dispersoids. Aging: 125–200°C × 2–48h (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017).

### 2.8 Oak Ridge / Eck Industries — Al–Ce Alloys

WO2018052517A9 (Weiss, priority 2016) broadly claims Al with 4–20 wt% rare-earth (Ce, La, mischmetal), optional Mg ≤15, Si ≤12, Fe ≤6, Ni ≤8, Cu ≤8. Examples: Al–8Ce–10Mg, Al–8Ce–4Si–1.5Mg–3Ni, Al–12Ce–4Si–0.4Mg (T6 UTS ~252 MPa, El 8.5%) (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033).

US12305267B2 (Rios/ORNL, granted) claims RE 5–30, Mg 0.4–12 wt%. Examples: Al–8Ce–0.4Mg, Al–12Ce–0.4Mg, Al–8Ce–8Mg (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000032).

### 2.9 Beijing University of Technology — Sc-Free Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr

This is a journal-published composition (Guo et al., Materials & Design 222, 2022, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2022.111064), not a patent. Composition: **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr wt%**. Primary L1₂ Al₃Zr nucleants create a bimodal grain structure; aging at 375°C/10h forms core–shell Al₃(Er,Zr) precipitates. As-built: YS 325±4, UTS 438±3 MPa, El 18±1.8%. **Aged: YS 440±3, UTS 520±2 MPa, El 15.5±1.0%** — matching Scalmalloy performance without Sc (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064).

### 2.10 Farkoosh — Al–Mn–Si–Sn High-Temperature Alloy

US12104237B2 (granted) claims (in at.%, not wt%) Mn 0.3–0.7, Si 0.2–1.0, Sn/In/Sb/Bi 0.01–0.02, optional Zr 0.01–0.1. α-Al(Mn,Fe)Si and Sn-rich nanoprecipitates provide high-temperature stability. Microhardness values up to 525–725 MPa reported (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000068, pqac-00000070).

### 2.11 Additional Families Not Fully Extracted

The following families were searched but patent-specific compositions and properties could not be fully extracted from the retrieved documents within the scope of this survey. These should be pursued in a follow-up:

- **Aeromet/AMT A20X (A205):** Al–Cu–Ag–Mg–Ti–B casting alloy adapted for AM. Known approximate composition: Al–4.5Cu–0.3Ag–0.3Mg–0.2Ti–0.02B.
- **Elementum 3D RAM alloys:** A6061-RAM2, A2024-RAM2, A7050-RAM2 with in-situ TiC ceramic inoculants.
- **Fehrmann AlMgty:** Al–Mg–Si high-Mg alloy for AM.
- **Rheinfelden, AMAG, Hydro, Trimet:** Commercial AlSi10Mg, Magsimal, Castasil variants.
- **Chalmers/Höganäs Al–Mn–Cr–Zr:** forAM powder grades.
- **EOS Al2139 AM, Al5X1, AlF357; SLM Solutions; Uniformity Labs; Mercury Marine Mercalloy.**
- **Japanese filings:** Toyo Aluminium, Daido, Kobe Steel, UACJ, Nippon Light Metal — Scalmalloy powder supply and proprietary compositions.
- **Chinese filings:** CRRC/Central South Al–Mg–Sc–Zr, Shanghai Jiao Tong TiB₂/AlSi10Mg composites.

---

## 3. Analysis: Questions A–D

The detailed analysis addressing white space, Sc-free performance benchmarking, seed experiments, and atomization guidance is presented in the following table:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### A. Composition Overlap and White Space

**Well-claimed regions (avoid as primary novelty):**
- Al–Mg–Sc–Zr(–Mn): Airbus Scalmalloy family (pqac-00000054)
- Al–Zn–Mg–Cu–Zr: HRL (pqac-00000046), Snyder (pqac-00000040), Croteau (pqac-00000048)
- Al–Fe–Zr: Constellium (pqac-00000041)
- Al–Ni–Mn–Fe–Zr–Ce: Rusal (pqac-00000010)
- Al–Mn–Sc: Monash/Amaero (pqac-00000018)
- Al–Mg–Zr (Sc-free): NanoAl (pqac-00000036)

**Apparent white space for Sc-free, little/no Zr compositions with Al ≥ 85 wt%:**
- **Al–Mn–Mg–Cr** (no Sc, no Zr): No retrieved LPBF-specific patent claims this four-element core. Approximately Mn 1.5–4, Mg 1–4, Cr 0.3–1 wt% appears open.
- **Al–Mn–Cr–Si** (no Sc, no Zr): Relatively open except for Farkoosh's nearby Al–Mn–Si–Sn claims at low atomic %.
- **Al–Cu–Mn–Cr–Mg** (no Sc, no Zr): Not covered by retrieved AM claims.
- **Al–Mg–Si–Cr–Ti** (no Sc, no Zr): Open, though Ti grain refinement effectiveness needs validation.
- **Al–Mn–Cr–Fe–Si** (no Sc, no Zr, no RE): Open for a low-cost thermally stable family.

### B. Highest Sc-Free Yield Strength at ≥8% Elongation

The best verified Sc-free result is **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr** from Beijing University of Technology (journal data): aged YS 440±3 MPa, UTS 520±2 MPa, El 15.5% (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064). However, this alloy contains 1.2 wt% Zr and 0.4 wt% Er. Among alloys with no Sc and no/low Zr, no commercial datasheet with verified tensile data meeting the ≥8% elongation criterion was recovered. The Rusal RS-553-type achieves only 5.3% elongation at room temperature (pqac-00000011).

### C. Recommended Seed Experiments

Given feedstock on hand (Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, small Sc and Er; Fe, Cu, Ni easy; Zr uncertain):

1. **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr** — Benchmark Sc-free recipe (requires Zr); age 375°C/10h (pqac-00000063).
2. **Al–4Mg–0.5Mn–0.3Sc–0.2Zr** — Low-Sc Scalmalloy control; age 300–325°C/4h (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055).
3. **Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–0.5Cr–0.1Ti** — **High-priority white-space seed**, Sc/Zr-free; Mn/Cr solid-solution + dispersoid strengthening with Ti grain control.
4. **Al–5Mg–0.8Mn–0.5Si–0.3Cr–0.05Sn** — Farkoosh-inspired Sc/Zr-free precipitation concept; run Sn-free and 0.02/0.05 Sn variants (pqac-00000047).
5. **Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–0.6Cr–0.4Si–0.05Sn** — Lead Zr-free candidate combining white-space motifs; factorially vary Cr 0.3/0.6, Si 0.2/0.4, Sn 0/0.05.
6. **Al–7Zn–3Mg–1Cu–0.1Ti** — High-risk 7xxx control without Zr; consider TiB₂ inoculation.

### D. Atomization and Processing Guidance from Patents

- **Nitrogen atomization:** Airbus EP2766136B1 claims 50–100 vol% N₂ in atomizing gas for Al–Mg–Sc–Zr powders, producing an AlN-rich surface passivation layer that dramatically reduces moisture uptake versus conventional Al₂O₃. Conventional gas must be ≥99.99% purity with H₂O ≤25 ppm (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054).
- **Mg/Zn vaporization loss:** HRL experimentally measured ~25% Zn and ~30% Mg loss during LPBF of 7075; enriched feedstock composition is claimed to compensate (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). These losses are machine- and parameter-specific.
- **Melt temperatures:** Croteau discloses melting at ~700–1000°C for Al–Zn–Mg–Zr alloys (pqac-00000049). For Zr/Cr/Mn-bearing melts, use master alloys and verify dissolution; superheat should be established from the specific alloy liquidus.
- **LPBF parameter windows:** Rusal used EOS M290 at 280–320W, 400–1200 mm/s, ≤45 µm layers (pqac-00000011). Monash used 370W, 1000 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers (pqac-00000019).
- **Build-plate preheat:** No specific build-plate preheat temperature was recovered from the aluminium AM patents surveyed, though the Monash patent notes that direct aging can be performed before or after removal from the build platform (pqac-00000022).
- **Crucible materials and ultrasonic atomization:** No aluminium-specific crucible recommendation or directly applicable ultrasonic atomization protocol was recovered from the patent literature surveyed.

---

## 4. Limitations and Recommended Follow-Up

This survey covers the major patent families identified through systematic searching but has the following limitations:

1. **Incomplete extraction** of some patent families (Constellium EP4149702A2 HT1 compositions, Elementum 3D RAM, Fehrmann AlMgty, Japanese and Chinese filings) due to retrieval and time constraints.
2. **White space assessment is provisional** — a formal freedom-to-operate search with claim charting is required before filing or committing to a composition.
3. **Commercial datasheets** (EOS, SLM Solutions, Uniformity Labs, Höganäs forAM, Equispheres) were not retrieved as full documents; published compositions from these sources should be obtained directly from vendors.
4. The A20X (Al–Cu–Ag–Mg–Ti–B) patent family was not retrieved; the known composition (~Al–4.5Cu–0.3Ag–0.3Mg–0.2Ti–0.02B) should be confirmed against the original Aeromet/AMT filings.

The core finding is that Sc-free, Zr-free or low-Zr aluminium alloys based on **Al–Mn–Mg–Cr(–Si)** combinations represent the most promising apparent white space for a discovery campaign using the available feedstocks, while compositions in the Al–Mg–Er–Zr system (if Zr is available) provide the strongest published Sc-free mechanical performance benchmarks."}

Survey the PATENT literature and COMMERCIAL products for aluminium alloys designed for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) and related powder routes, so that we can choose starting compositions for an alloy discovery campaign and know what is already claimed. We want published compositions, not marketing.

For each entry give: assignee / vendor, product name if any, patent or application numbers (US, EP, WO, CN, JP, DE), priority year, the claimed composition RANGES and the worked EXAMPLE compositions (wt%), the cracking-control and strengthening mechanism claimed, recommended heat treatment, the properties reported in the patent or datasheet (yield, UTS, elongation, hardness, conductivity, test orientation), and whether the patent is granted, pending, expired or abandoned where known.

Cover at least:
1. Airbus / APWorks Scalmalloy (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr-Mn), and the earlier Al-Mg-Sc family patents; lower-Sc or Sc-free variants claimed by others.
2. HRL Laboratories 7A77 and Zr / grain-refiner functionalized 7xxx, 6xxx, 2xxx powders.
3. Aeromet / Aluminium Materials Technologies A20X (A205; Al-Cu-Ag-Mg-Ti-B).
4. NanoAl / Unity Aluminum / Braidy Addalloy (Al-Mg-Zr and others) and Northwestern University Al-Zr-(Er, Sc, Yb, Si) patents.
5. Constellium Aheadd CP1 (Al-Fe-Zr) and HT1 (Al-Ni-Mn-Cu-Zr-Fe class), and the C-TEC patent families (Al-Zr, Al-Fe-Zr, Al-Ni-Zr, Al-Mn-Zr, Al-Cr-Zr).
6. Fehrmann AlMgty (Al-Mg-Si / high-Mg), Rheinfelden (Magsimal, Castasil, Castaduct for AM), AMAG, Hydro, Trimet.
7. Elementum 3D A1000-RAM, A2024-RAM2, A6061-RAM2, A7050-RAM2 (reactive additive manufacturing, in-situ ceramic inoculants).
8. Rusal / IL&M (RS-230, RS-300, RS-320, RS-333, RS-390, RS-553 and similar: Al-Si-Mg-Cu, Al-Mg-Sc, Al-Ni-Mn-Fe-Zr, Al-Cu-Ce), with compositions.
9. Monash University / Amaero high-strength Al-Mn-Sc ("HOT Al"), and Al-Mg-Si-Sc-Zr.
10. Chalmers / Hoganas Al-Mn-Cr-Zr; Hoganas forAM Al grades; Kymera / ECKA / AP&C / Equispheres / Valimet / Carpenter / Sandvik / Toyal / Eckart (e.g. Eckart TiB2- or Zr-modified, Toyal Hyper-Al) aluminium AM powders with published chemistries.
11. Oak Ridge / Eck Industries / Ames Al-Ce alloys (Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Ce-Ni-Mn, Al-Cu-Mn-Zr / ACMZ, DuAlumin-3D), Lawrence Livermore Al-Ce.
12. Alcoa / Arconic / Howmet AM aluminium (Al-Fe-V-Si, Al-Ni, Al-Mn, "A1000" class), QuesTek Al for AM (Sc-free, high-temperature), Citrine / HRL / NASA collaborations, NASA 7xxx / GRCop is out of scope.
13. Japanese and Korean filings: Toyo Aluminium, Daido, Kobe Steel, UACJ, Nippon Light Metal, Sumitomo, Hitachi Metals, Toyota (Al-Fe, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Ni-Co, Al-Mn-Cr, Al-Si-Mg-Mn high-Mg).
14. Chinese filings and products: CRRC / Central South University Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, Al-Mg-Er-Zr (Beijing University of Technology Er-microalloying patents), Al-Mn-Mg-Er-Zr, TiB2/AlSi10Mg (Shanghai Jiao Tong), Al-Zn-Mg-Sc-Zr, Sc-free high-strength Al for AM.
15. EOS (Al2139 AM, Al5X1, AlF357), SLM Solutions / Nikon SLM, 3D Systems (A6061-RAM2 licence), Colibrium / GE Additive, Mercury Marine (Mercalloy A362 for AM), Gränges (Dispal-type Al-Si-Fe-Ni), PEAK Werkstoff / Erbslöh (Dispal S220/S250 Al-Si), Kaiser, Novelis, Uniformity Labs.
16. Any patents specifically on aluminium powders made by ULTRASONIC atomization or small-batch atomization for alloy development.

Then answer:
A. Which claimed composition windows overlap a search space of Al >= 85 wt% with a few additions from Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn? Where is there apparent white space (combinations nobody has claimed or published), especially Sc-free and with little or no Zr?
B. Which commercial Sc-free alloys have the highest reported yield strength at >= 8 % elongation, and what do their datasheets give for as-built versus heat-treated?
C. Which patent example compositions would make good seed experiments for us, given feedstock on hand (Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, small Sc and Er; Fe, Cu and Ni easy to buy; Zr uncertain)?
D. Anything in these patents about atomization practice (melt temperature, superheat for Zr/Ti/Cr/Mn-bearing melts, crucible materials, Mg loss) or about build-plate preheat that we should copy.

Give patent numbers and URLs or DOIs for every claim. Say clearly when a composition comes from a datasheet, a patent example, a patent claim range, or a journal paper by the same group.

# Survey of Aluminium Alloys Designed for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF/SLM): Patent and Commercial Landscape

## 1. Introduction

This survey covers the patent and published-composition landscape for aluminium alloys specifically designed or adapted for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) and related rapid-solidification powder routes. The objective is to identify claimed composition windows, worked example compositions, strengthening mechanisms, recommended heat treatments, and reported mechanical properties, so that starting compositions for a new alloy discovery campaign can be selected with knowledge of what is already claimed. The following sections are organized by alloy family, followed by an integrated analysis addressing white space, best Sc-free performers, recommended seed experiments, and atomization/processing guidance.

---

## 2. Major Alloy Families — Compositions, Patents, Properties

### 2.1 Airbus / APWorks — Scalmalloy® (Al–Mg–Sc–Zr–Mn)

The foundational Scalmalloy® patent family originates from Palm / EADS Deutschland GmbH, with the earliest priority around 2007 (WO2008/125092, DE102007018123). The atomization-related patent EP2766136B1 (priority 2011) claims nitrogen-rich atomization (50–100 vol% N₂) of Al–Sc alloys with the composition Mg 0.5–10, Sc 0.2–2.0, Zr 0.2–2.0 wt%, optionally with Mn 0.1–1.0, and a preferred sub-range of Mg 2.5–5.0, Sc 0.3–1.0, Zr 0.2–0.5, Mn 0.1–0.8 wt% (EP2766136B1 pages 3-5). The published Scalmalloy® composition used in research is Al–4.4Mg–0.8Sc–0.3Zr–0.5Mn wt% (schimback2022alloydesignstrategy pages 1-2). The composition range reported across studies is Mg 3.02–4.77, Sc 0.20–0.71, Mn 0.20–0.53, Zr 0.08–0.42 wt% (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 2-5).

**Mechanism:** Primary Al₃(Sc,Zr) particles nucleate fine equiaxed grains at melt-pool boundaries, creating a bimodal microstructure that suppresses hot cracking. Direct aging precipitates coherent L1₂ Al₃(Sc,Zr) nanoprecipitates for strengthening (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 1-2, cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 16-18).

**Properties (journal/review data):** As-built YS 256–278 MPa, UTS 349–350 MPa, El 19–20%; after direct aging at 325°C × 4 h: YS 456–469 MPa, UTS 512–521 MPa, El 12–13%; after HIP at 325°C/1000 bar: YS 482–493 MPa, UTS 523–547 MPa (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 1-2, mehta2021laserpowderbed pages 7-10).

Airbus also developed **Scancromal®** (Al–2.6Cr–0.7Sc–0.3Zr, US20220186346A1) and **Scantital®** (Al–1.0Ti–1.0Sc–0.4Zr, US20220168811A1 with Ti 0.1–15, Sc 0.1–3.0, Zr 0.1–3.0 wt%) (schimback2022alloydesignstrategy pages 1-2, US20220168811A1 pages 4-5).

### 2.2 HRL Laboratories — Functionalized 7xxx/6xxx and 7A77-Type

HRL's core innovation is surface functionalization of conventional alloy powders with grain-refining nanoparticles. Key granted patents include US11053571B2, US11286543B2, and US11919085B2 (priority 2015–2017 family). The worked example uses Al 7075 powder (Al bal.–5.40Zn–2.25Mg–1.54Cu–0.19Cr–0.17Fe–0.13Si wt%) with ~1 vol% ZrH₂ nanoparticles (500–1500 nm), producing crack-free equiaxed microstructures via Al₃Zr heterogeneous nucleation (US11919085B2 pages 31-34, US20240082913A1 pages 64-66, US11053571B2 pages 32-33). T6 heat treatment: 480°C/2h, water quench, 120°C/18h (US11286543B2 pages 32-33).

The **7A77-type enriched feedstock** patent US11578389B2 (priority 2017, granted) claims a feedstock with Al 79.8–88.3, Cu 1.1–2.1, Mg 3.0–4.6, Zn 7.1–9.0, Zr 0.5–2.8 wt%, designed so that after ~25% Zn and ~30% Mg vaporization loss during LPBF, the printed part reaches Al 84.5–92.1, Cu 1.1–2.1, Mg 1.8–2.9, Zn 4.5–6.1, Zr 0.5–2.8 wt% (US11578389B2 pages 7-10, US11578389B2 pages 30-33).

### A. Composition Overlap and White Space

**Well-claimed regions (avoid as primary novelty):**
- Al–Mg–Sc–Zr(–Mn): Airbus Scalmalloy family (EP2766136B1 pages 3-5)
- Al–Zn–Mg–Cu–Zr: HRL (US11578389B2 pages 30-33), Snyder (US10941473B2 pages 21-22), Croteau (US20210254196A1 pages 11-12)
- Al–Fe–Zr: Constellium (WO2020095009A2 pages 1-4)
- Al–Ni–Mn–Fe–Zr–Ce: Rusal (CA3162961C pages 1-3)
- Al–Mn–Sc: Monash/Amaero (US11976343B2 pages 7-9)
- Al–Mg–Zr (Sc-free): NanoAl (US11603583B2 pages 18-20)

**Apparent white space for Sc-free, little/no Zr compositions with Al ≥ 85 wt%:**
- **Al–Mn–Mg–Cr** (no Sc, no Zr): No retrieved LPBF-specific patent claims this four-element core. Approximately Mn 1.5–4, Mg 1–4, Cr 0.3–1 wt% appears open.
- **Al–Mn–Cr–Si** (no Sc, no Zr): Relatively open except for Farkoosh's nearby Al–Mn–Si–Sn claims at low atomic %.
- **Al–Cu–Mn–Cr–Mg** (no Sc, no Zr): Not covered by retrieved AM claims.
- **Al–Mg–Si–Cr–Ti** (no Sc, no Zr): Open, though Ti grain refinement effectiveness needs validation.
- **Al–Mn–Cr–Fe–Si** (no Sc, no Zr, no RE): Open for a low-cost thermally stable family.

### B. Highest Sc-Free Yield Strength at ≥8% Elongation

The best verified Sc-free result is **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr** from Beijing University of Technology (journal data): aged YS 440±3 MPa, UTS 520±2 MPa, El 15.5% (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 10-11, guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). However, this alloy contains 1.2 wt% Zr and 0.4 wt% Er. Among alloys with no Sc and no/low Zr, no commercial datasheet with verified tensile data meeting the ≥8% elongation criterion was recovered. The Rusal RS-553-type achieves only 5.3% elongation at room temperature (CA3162961C pages 8-9).

### C. Recommended Seed Experiments

Given feedstock on hand (Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, small Sc and Er; Fe, Cu, Ni easy; Zr uncertain):

1. **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr** — Benchmark Sc-free recipe (requires Zr); age 375°C/10h (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 10-11).
2. **Al–4Mg–0.5Mn–0.3Sc–0.2Zr** — Low-Sc Scalmalloy control; age 300–325°C/4h (EP2766136B1 pages 3-5, cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 1-2).
3. **Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–0.5Cr–0.1Ti** — **High-priority white-space seed**, Sc/Zr-free; Mn/Cr solid-solution + dispersoid strengthening with Ti grain control.
4. **Al–5Mg–0.8Mn–0.5Si–0.3Cr–0.05Sn** — Farkoosh-inspired Sc/Zr-free precipitation concept; run Sn-free and 0.02/0.05 Sn variants (US12104237B2 pages 1-4).
5. **Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–0.6Cr–0.4Si–0.05Sn** — Lead Zr-free candidate combining white-space motifs; factorially vary Cr 0.3/0.6, Si 0.2/0.4, Sn 0/0.05.
6. **Al–7Zn–3Mg–1Cu–0.1Ti** — High-risk 7xxx control without Zr; consider TiB₂ inoculation.

### D. Atomization and Processing Guidance from Patents

- **Nitrogen atomization:** Airbus EP2766136B1 claims 50–100 vol% N₂ in atomizing gas for Al–Mg–Sc–Zr powders, producing an AlN-rich surface passivation layer that dramatically reduces moisture uptake versus conventional Al₂O₃. Conventional gas must be ≥99.99% purity with H₂O ≤25 ppm (EP2766136B1 pages 2-3, EP2766136B1 pages 3-5).
- **Mg/Zn vaporization loss:** HRL experimentally measured ~25% Zn and ~30% Mg loss during LPBF of 7075; enriched feedstock composition is claimed to compensate (US11578389B2 pages 7-10, US11578389B2 pages 30-33). These losses are machine- and parameter-specific.
- **Melt temperatures:** Croteau discloses melting at ~700–1000°C for Al–Zn–Mg–Zr alloys (US20210254196A1 pages 1-10). For Zr/Cr/Mn-bearing melts, use master alloys and verify dissolution; superheat should be established from the specific alloy liquidus.
- **LPBF parameter windows:** Rusal used EOS M290 at 280–320W, 400–1200 mm/s, ≤45 µm layers (CA3162961C pages 8-9). Monash used 370W, 1000 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers (US11976343B2 pages 14-16).
- **Build-plate preheat:** No specific build-plate preheat temperature was recovered from the aluminium AM patents surveyed, though the Monash patent notes that direct aging can be performed before or after removal from the build platform (US11976343B2 pages 1-4).
- **Crucible materials and ultrasonic atomization:** No aluminium-specific crucible recommendation or directly applicable ultrasonic atomization protocol was recovered from the patent literature surveyed.

---

## 4. Limitations and Recommended Follow-Up

This survey covers the major patent families identified through systematic searching but has the following limitations:

1. **Incomplete extraction** of some patent families (Constellium EP4149702A2 HT1 compositions, Elementum 3D RAM, Fehrmann AlMgty, Japanese and Chinese filings) due to retrieval and time constraints.
2. **White space assessment is provisional** — a formal freedom-to-operate search with claim charting is required before filing or committing to a composition.
3. **Commercial datasheets** (EOS, SLM Solutions, Uniformity Labs, Höganäs forAM, Equispheres) were not retrieved as full documents; published compositions from these sources should be obtained directly from vendors.
4. The A20X (Al–Cu–Ag–Mg–Ti–B) patent family was not retrieved; the known composition (~Al–4.5Cu–0.3Ag–0.3Mg–0.2Ti–0.02B) should be confirmed against the original Aeromet/AMT filings.

The core finding is that Sc-free, Zr-free or low-Zr aluminium alloys based on **Al–Mn–Mg–Cr(–Si)** combinations represent the most promising apparent white space for a discovery campaign using the available feedstocks, while compositions in the Al–Mg–Er–Zr system (if Zr is available) provide the strongest published Sc-free mechanical performance benchmarks.

### 2.1 Airbus / APWorks — Scalmalloy® (Al–Mg–Sc–Zr–Mn)

The foundational Scalmalloy® patent family originates from Palm / EADS Deutschland GmbH, with the earliest priority around 2007 (WO2008/125092, DE102007018123). The atomization-related patent EP2766136B1 (priority 2011) claims nitrogen-rich atomization (50–100 vol% N₂) of Al–Sc alloys with the composition Mg 0.5–10, Sc 0.2–2.0, Zr 0.2–2.0 wt%, optionally with Mn 0.1–1.0, and a preferred sub-range of Mg 2.5–5.0, Sc 0.3–1.0, Zr 0.2–0.5, Mn 0.1–0.8 wt% (pqac-00000054). The published Scalmalloy® composition used in research is Al–4.4Mg–0.8Sc–0.3Zr–0.5Mn wt% (pqac-00000000). The composition range reported across studies is Mg 3.02–4.77, Sc 0.20–0.71, Mn 0.20–0.53, Zr 0.08–0.42 wt% (pqac-00000057).

**Mechanism:** Primary Al₃(Sc,Zr) particles nucleate fine equiaxed grains at melt-pool boundaries, creating a bimodal microstructure that suppresses hot cracking. Direct aging precipitates coherent L1₂ Al₃(Sc,Zr) nanoprecipitates for strengthening (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000060).

**Properties (journal/review data):** As-built YS 256–278 MPa, UTS 349–350 MPa, El 19–20%; after direct aging at 325°C × 4 h: YS 456–469 MPa, UTS 512–521 MPa, El 12–13%; after HIP at 325°C/1000 bar: YS 482–493 MPa, UTS 523–547 MPa (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056).

Airbus also developed **Scancromal®** (Al–2.6Cr–0.7Sc–0.3Zr, US20220186346A1) and **Scantital®** (Al–1.0Ti–1.0Sc–0.4Zr, US20220168811A1 with Ti 0.1–15, Sc 0.1–3.0, Zr 0.1–3.0 wt%) (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028).

### 2.2 HRL Laboratories — Functionalized 7xxx/6xxx and 7A77-Type

HRL's core innovation is surface functionalization of conventional alloy powders with grain-refining nanoparticles. Key granted patents include US11053571B2, US11286543B2, and US11919085B2 (priority 2015–2017 family). The worked example uses Al 7075 powder (Al bal.–5.40Zn–2.25Mg–1.54Cu–0.19Cr–0.17Fe–0.13Si wt%) with ~1 vol% ZrH₂ nanoparticles (500–1500 nm), producing crack-free equiaxed microstructures via Al₃Zr heterogeneous nucleation (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006). T6 heat treatment: 480°C/2h, water quench, 120°C/18h (pqac-00000007).

The **7A77-type enriched feedstock** patent US11578389B2 (priority 2017, granted) claims a feedstock with Al 79.8–88.3, Cu 1.1–2.1, Mg 3.0–4.6, Zn 7.1–9.0, Zr 0.5–2.8 wt%, designed so that after ~25% Zn and ~30% Mg vaporization loss during LPBF, the printed part reaches Al 84.5–92.1, Cu 1.1–2.1, Mg 1.8–2.9, Zn 4.5–6.1, Zr 0.5–2.8 wt% (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

*Table: Evidence-ranked overlap, apparent white space, Sc-free performance, seed compositions, and process guidance for an LPBF aluminium discovery campaign. “White space” is provisional and requires a formal claim chart and broader freedom-to-operate search.*

### A. Composition Overlap and White Space

**Well-claimed regions (avoid as primary novelty):**
- Al–Mg–Sc–Zr(–Mn): Airbus Scalmalloy family (pqac-00000054)
- Al–Zn–Mg–Cu–Zr: HRL (pqac-00000046), Snyder (pqac-00000040), Croteau (pqac-00000048)
- Al–Fe–Zr: Constellium (pqac-00000041)
- Al–Ni–Mn–Fe–Zr–Ce: Rusal (pqac-00000010)
- Al–Mn–Sc: Monash/Amaero (pqac-00000018)
- Al–Mg–Zr (Sc-free): NanoAl (pqac-00000036)

**Apparent white space for Sc-free, little/no Zr compositions with Al ≥ 85 wt%:**
- **Al–Mn–Mg–Cr** (no Sc, no Zr): No retrieved LPBF-specific patent claims this four-element core. Approximately Mn 1.5–4, Mg 1–4, Cr 0.3–1 wt% appears open.
- **Al–Mn–Cr–Si** (no Sc, no Zr): Relatively open except for Farkoosh's nearby Al–Mn–Si–Sn claims at low atomic %.
- **Al–Cu–Mn–Cr–Mg** (no Sc, no Zr): Not covered by retrieved AM claims.
- **Al–Mg–Si–Cr–Ti** (no Sc, no Zr): Open, though Ti grain refinement effectiveness needs validation.
- **Al–Mn–Cr–Fe–Si** (no Sc, no Zr, no RE): Open for a low-cost thermally stable family.

### B. Highest Sc-Free Yield Strength at ≥8% Elongation

The best verified Sc-free result is **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr** from Beijing University of Technology (journal data): aged YS 440±3 MPa, UTS 520±2 MPa, El 15.5% (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064). However, this alloy contains 1.2 wt% Zr and 0.4 wt% Er. Among alloys with no Sc and no/low Zr, no commercial datasheet with verified tensile data meeting the ≥8% elongation criterion was recovered. The Rusal RS-553-type achieves only 5.3% elongation at room temperature (pqac-00000011).

### C. Recommended Seed Experiments

Given feedstock on hand (Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, small Sc and Er; Fe, Cu, Ni easy; Zr uncertain):

1. **Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.2Zr** — Benchmark Sc-free recipe (requires Zr); age 375°C/10h (pqac-00000063).
2. **Al–4Mg–0.5Mn–0.3Sc–0.2Zr** — Low-Sc Scalmalloy control; age 300–325°C/4h (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055).
3. **Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–0.5Cr–0.1Ti** — **High-priority white-space seed**, Sc/Zr-free; Mn/Cr solid-solution + dispersoid strengthening with Ti grain control.
4. **Al–5Mg–0.8Mn–0.5Si–0.3Cr–0.05Sn** — Farkoosh-inspired Sc/Zr-free precipitation concept; run Sn-free and 0.02/0.05 Sn variants (pqac-00000047).
5. **Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–0.6Cr–0.4Si–0.05Sn** — Lead Zr-free candidate combining white-space motifs; factorially vary Cr 0.3/0.6, Si 0.2/0.4, Sn 0/0.05.
6. **Al–7Zn–3Mg–1Cu–0.1Ti** — High-risk 7xxx control without Zr; consider TiB₂ inoculation.

### D. Atomization and Processing Guidance from Patents

- **Nitrogen atomization:** Airbus EP2766136B1 claims 50–100 vol% N₂ in atomizing gas for Al–Mg–Sc–Zr powders, producing an AlN-rich surface passivation layer that dramatically reduces moisture uptake versus conventional Al₂O₃. Conventional gas must be ≥99.99% purity with H₂O ≤25 ppm (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054).
- **Mg/Zn vaporization loss:** HRL experimentally measured ~25% Zn and ~30% Mg loss during LPBF of 7075; enriched feedstock composition is claimed to compensate (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). These losses are machine- and parameter-specific.
- **Melt temperatures:** Croteau discloses melting at ~700–1000°C for Al–Zn–Mg–Zr alloys (pqac-00000049). For Zr/Cr/Mn-bearing melts, use master alloys and verify dissolution; superheat should be established from the specific alloy liquidus.
- **LPBF parameter windows:** Rusal used EOS M290 at 280–320W, 400–1200 mm/s, ≤45 µm layers (pqac-00000011). Monash used 370W, 1000 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers (pqac-00000019).
- **Build-plate preheat:** No specific build-plate preheat temperature was recovered from the aluminium AM patents surveyed, though the Monash patent notes that direct aging can be performed before or after removal from the build platform (pqac-00000022).
- **Crucible materials and ultrasonic atomization:** No aluminium-specific crucible recommendation or directly applicable ultrasonic atomization protocol was recovered from the patent literature surveyed.

---

## 4. Limitations and Recommended Follow-Up

This survey covers the major patent families identified through systematic searching but has the following limitations:

1. **Incomplete extraction** of some patent families (Constellium EP4149702A2 HT1 compositions, Elementum 3D RAM, Fehrmann AlMgty, Japanese and Chinese filings) due to retrieval and time constraints.
2. **White space assessment is provisional** — a formal freedom-to-operate search with claim charting is required before filing or committing to a composition.
3. **Commercial datasheets** (EOS, SLM Solutions, Uniformity Labs, Höganäs forAM, Equispheres) were not retrieved as full documents; published compositions from these sources should be obtained directly from vendors.
4. The A20X (Al–Cu–Ag–Mg–Ti–B) patent family was not retrieved; the known composition (~Al–4.5Cu–0.3Ag–0.3Mg–0.2Ti–0.02B) should be confirmed against the original Aeromet/AMT filings.

The core finding is that Sc-free, Zr-free or low-Zr aluminium alloys based on **Al–Mn–Mg–Cr(–Si)** combinations represent the most promising apparent white space for a discovery campaign using the available feedstocks, while compositions in the Al–Mg–Er–Zr system (if Zr is available) provide the strongest published Sc-free mechanical performance benchmarks.

Example 1 used inert-gas-atomized powder and EOS M280 powder-bed fusion. The starting powder contained 8.14 wt.% Fe, 1.48 wt.% V, 1.66 wt.% Si, and 2.10 wt.% Cu, balance Al and impurities. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the invention as an Al–Mn–Sc alloy for additive manufacturing and other rapid-solidification processes, with zirconium also discussed as an alloying addition. The explicitly stated manganese range is 2.01–15.0 wt%; the excerpt does not provide the complete claimed composition ranges for aluminium, scandium, zirconium, or other elements. It explains that rapid cooling, including laser remelting, traps manganese and scandium in supersaturated solid solution and prevents formation of visible primary Al6Mn or Al3Sc precipitates in the remelted zone. Worked Examples 1 and 2, illustrated by Figures 1–4, include laser-remelted material and tensile samples made by the disclosed process. Laser-remelted regions achieved 170–186 HV0.5 hardness, retaining these levels after 168 hours at 300°C, demonstrating thermal stability. Tensile testing reportedly gave 427 MPa yield strength in the as-fabricated condition and 577 MPa after heat treatment. The preferred heat treatment is simple and preferably single-stage, serving both stress relief and precipitation hardening, without the solution-treatment step required by some other precipitation-hardening aluminium alloys. For SLM-built parts, it may be performed before or after removal from the build platform.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Al–Mn–Sc alloys intended for rapid-solidification and additive-manufacturing processing, but it does not provide the complete claimed composition ranges; it only states that certain other elements should be below 4 wt% individually and 15 wt% total. The worked compositions are: (1) Al–4.18Mn–2Mg–0.9Sc–0.18Zr, (2) Al–3Mn–1.5Mg–1Sc–0.05Zr, and (3) gas-atomized powder at Al–4.52Mn–1.32Mg–0.79Sc–0.74Zr, with balance aluminum. The first two were melted from master alloys, cast and cooled at approximately 10^3 K/s, then laser-remelted using SLM conditions of 370 W, 500 mm/s, 0.1 mm spot and 0.1 mm hatch. After ageing at 300 °C, maximum hardness was 186.3±2 HV0.5 after 10 h for alloy 1 and 170.6±2 HV0.5 after 24 h for alloy 2. Prism samples of composition 3 were SLM-built at 370 W, 1000 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch and 30 μm layers. As-built tensile properties were 427 MPa yield strength, 453 MPa UTS and 12.0% elongation. Treatment at 300±2 °C for 5 h increased these to 577 MPa yield strength and 588 MPa UTS, with 11.3% elongation. More generally, post-treatment is described as 200–500 °C for 0.10–100 h, preferably direct ageing, with HIP also applicable.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not identify or reproduce US20220168811A1 or US20220186346A1, nor does it provide their claimed composition ranges or patent-specific worked examples. It does, however, report representative compositions of scandium-modified aluminium alloys developed for laser powder bed fusion. The principal examples are: an Al-Mg-Sc-Zr-Mn alloy (Scalmalloy®) containing 4.4 wt.% Mg, 0.8 wt.% Sc, 0.3 wt.% Zr, and 0.5 wt.% Mn, with aluminium as the balance; an Al-Cr-Sc-Zr alloy (Scancromal®) containing 2.6 wt.% Cr, 0.7 wt.% Sc, and 0.3 wt.% Zr, with aluminium as the balance; and an Al-Ti-Sc-Zr alloy (Scantital®) containing 1.0 wt.% Ti, 1.0 wt.% Sc, and 0.4 wt.% Zr, with aluminium as the balance. A binary Al-Sc-Zr base alloy is also listed with 1.0 wt.% Sc and 0.4 wt.% Zr. The article associates the Cr-rich composition with epitaxial grain growth and texture across several weld tracks, while the Mg-containing alloy forms a bimodal microstructure and the Ti-containing alloy forms a uniform ultrafine-grained structure. These are experimental alloy examples, not patent composition ranges.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not discuss the Constellium Chehab patents WO2020095009A2 or EP3914748B1, and it provides no iron-containing alloy composition ranges specifically attributable to those patents. It does, however, describe related rapidly solidified aluminum–magnesium–zirconium alloys for additive manufacturing. The disclosed general composition is 1–10 wt.% magnesium, 0.3–3 wt.% zirconium (preferably 0.45–3 wt.%), optional 0.3–1.5 wt.% vanadium, with aluminum as the balance. The alloys contain both fine Al3Zr primary precipitates, reported at approximately 0.05–1.5 μm in diameter, and L12-structured Al3Zr nanoprecipitates approximately 3–50 nm in diameter. Example materials include Al-3.6Mg-1.2Zr wt.% powder used to produce 3D-printed components, including specimens aged at 400°C for 8 or 144 hours. Other reported examples are Al-4Mg-1.7Zr wt.% and melt-spun Al-4.5Mg-0.2Zr and Al-4.5Mg-0.5Zr compositions. The reported properties include high strength and ductility, creep and heat resistance up to about 400°C, corrosion resistance, weldability, precipitation strengthening, grain refinement, and strength comparable to analogous Al–Mg–Sc alloys. Rapid solidification enables zirconium levels above conventional casting limits by suppressing coarse primary Al3Zr formation.
